title: Indian Polity & Constitution
summary: The Constitution — its making, Preamble, Parts and Schedules, Rights, the three organs of government, amendments and constitutional bodies. CGL consistently asks 3-4 factual one-liners here, the single most predictable GA block.

subtopics.title: Making of the Constitution & borrowed features
subtopics.concept:
The Constituent Assembly was formed under the **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)**; its members were indirectly elected by provincial assemblies. It first met on **9 December 1946** in the Central Hall of Parliament with **Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha** as temporary chairman. **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** was elected permanent President (11 Dec 1946); **H.C. Mukherjee** was Vice-President; **Sir B.N. Rau** was the Constitutional Adviser. Nehru's **Objective Resolution (13 Dec 1946)** became the basis of the Preamble.

### Key facts (asked again and again)
| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| Time taken | 2 years, 11 months, 18 days (11 sessions) |
| Adopted | **26 November 1949** (Constitution Day / Samvidhan Divas) |
| Came into force | **26 January 1950** (marks Purna Swaraj Day, Lahore Session 1929) |
| Members | 389 originally, 299 after Partition; **284 signed** (24 Jan 1950) |
| Drafting Committee (29 Aug 1947) | **7 members**, chairman **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** |
| Handwritten by | Prem Behari Narain Raizada; seal showed an **Elephant** |
| Cost | About ₹64 lakh (then) |

### Important committees of the Assembly
| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| Union Powers, Union Constitution, States Committees | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| Provincial Constitution Committee; Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities | Sardar Patel |
| Rules of Procedure, Steering Committee, Flag Committee | Rajendra Prasad |
| Drafting Committee | B.R. Ambedkar |

### Borrowed features (very common PYQ)
| Source country | Features borrowed |
|---|---|
| **UK** | Parliamentary government, Rule of Law, single citizenship, Cabinet system, writs, bicameralism |
| **USA** | Fundamental Rights, judicial review, impeachment of President, independent judiciary, Preamble ideal |
| **Ireland** | Directive Principles (DPSP), method of electing the President, nomination of 12 members to Rajya Sabha |
| **Canada** | Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with Centre, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of SC |
| **Australia** | Concurrent List, freedom of inter-state trade and commerce, joint sitting of the two Houses |
| **USSR (Russia)** | Fundamental Duties, ideal of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble |
| **France** | Republic, ideals of liberty, equality, fraternity |
| **Germany (Weimar)** | Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency |
| **South Africa** | Procedure for amendment, election of Rajya Sabha members |
| **Japan** | Concept of "procedure established by law" |

tricks.title: Committee-chairman pairing
tricks.body: **Nehru** took the *Union/States/Constitution* committees (the 'national' subjects), **Patel** took *Provinces and Rights* (the 'practical' subjects), **Prasad** took *procedure and flag*, **Ambedkar** took the *Drafting* pen.

example.q: Who chaired the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities?
example.solution: Sardar Patel — 'Rights' belong to Patel's practical cluster.

tricks.title: Borrowed features speed-pair
tricks.body: UK-Parliament • USA-Rights • Ireland-Duties-of-state (DPSP) • Canada-Centre-strong • Australia-List-3 • USSR-Duties-of-citizens • France-Republic • Germany-Emergency-rights • Japan-law-procedure.

example.q: Fundamental Duties are inspired by which constitution?
example.solution: USSR (Russia); the DPSP counterpart from Ireland.

mistakes: Confusing adoption date (26 Nov 1949) with enforcement date (26 Jan 1950).
Assuming Ambedkar presided over the Assembly — Rajendra Prasad did; Ambedkar chaired only the Drafting Committee.
Attributing joint sitting to Canada instead of Australia.
subtopics.notes:
### The Assembly that wrote the Constitution
India's Constituent Assembly was formed in **1946** under the **Cabinet Mission Plan**. Its members were **indirectly elected** by the provincial assemblies through proportional representation. The sanctioned strength was **389** — 292 from British provinces, 93 from princely states and 4 from chief commissioners' provinces; after Partition it came down to **299**. It first met on **9 December 1946** in the Central Hall of Parliament. **Dr Sachchidananda Sinha** presided as temporary chairman. **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was elected permanent President on **11 December 1946**, with **H.C. Mukherjee** as Vice-President. **Sir B.N. Rau** was the constitutional adviser who prepared the first draft that the Drafting Committee reworked.

### The clock of key dates
| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 13 Dec 1946 | **Objectives Resolution** moved by **Nehru**; adopted **22 Jan 1947** — the seed of the Preamble |
| 29 Aug 1947 | **Drafting Committee** formed — **7 members**, chaired by **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** |
| 4 Nov 1948 | Draft Constitution introduced in the Assembly |
| 26 Nov 1949 | Constitution **adopted** (now Constitution Day) |
| 24 Jan 1950 | **284 members signed**; 'Jana Gana Mana' adopted as anthem |
| 26 Jan 1950 | Constitution **came into force** (Republic Day) |

The Assembly took **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**, held **11 sessions**, and the whole exercise cost about **₹64 lakh**. It then served as the **provisional Parliament** until the first general election (1951-52). 26 January was chosen to honour **Purna Swaraj Day** (26 Jan 1930), the day the Congress had demanded complete independence (decided at the Lahore session, Dec 1929).

### Committee ↔ chairman (asked again and again)
| Committee | Chairman |
|---|---|
| Union Powers Committee; Union Constitution Committee; States Committee | **Jawaharlal Nehru** |
| Provincial Constitution Committee; Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities | **Sardar Patel** |
| Rules of Procedure; Steering Committee; Flag Committee | **Rajendra Prasad** |
| **Drafting Committee** | **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** |

The rough division: **Nehru** took the 'national' committees, **Patel** the 'practical/state' ones, **Prasad** the procedural ones, **Ambedkar** the drafting pen.

### Borrowed features — the source map
| Feature | Borrowed from |
|---|---|
| Federal scheme, Governors, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions, administrative detail | **Government of India Act, 1935** (the single biggest source) |
| Parliamentary system, rule of law, single citizenship, cabinet, legislative procedure, bicameralism, writs | **Britain** |
| Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of judiciary, impeachment of the President, Vice-President as Rajya Sabha chairman, removal of judges | **USA** |
| Directive Principles, method of President's election, nomination of 12 members to Rajya Sabha | **Ireland** |
| Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, appointment of Governors, advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court | **Canada** |
| Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce, **joint sitting** of the two Houses | **Australia** |
| Fundamental Duties, the ideal of justice (social, economic, political) in the Preamble | **USSR** |
| Ideals of liberty, equality, fraternity in the Preamble; Republic | **France** |
| Suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency | **Germany (Weimar)** |
| Procedure for amendment; election of Rajya Sabha members | **South Africa** |
| 'Procedure established by law' (Art 21 wording) | **Japan** |

### Quick revision
- Cabinet Mission Plan 1946; indirect election; 389 seats → 299 after Partition.
- 9 Dec 1946 first meeting; Sinha temporary chair; Rajendra Prasad permanent President; B.N. Rau adviser.
- Drafting Committee 29 Aug 1947, 7 members, Ambedkar chairman.
- Adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950 (Purna Swaraj Day 1930); 2y-11m-18d; 11 sessions; ₹64 lakh.
- Nehru — Objectives Resolution; union committees. Patel — provinces + rights. Prasad — rules/flag/steering.
- Biggest source = Government of India Act 1935; DPSP-Ireland, FRs-USA, Duties-USSR, joint sitting-Australia.

patterns.name: Assembly: people, dates and numbers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who was the temporary/permanent President of the Constituent Assembly', 'when did it first meet', 'how long did it take', 'how many members signed'.
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the four anchors: 9 Dec 1946 (first meeting), 26 Nov 1949 (adopted), 24 Jan 1950 (284 signed), 26 Jan 1950 (in force).
2. People: Sinha = temporary chairman, Rajendra Prasad = permanent President, H.C. Mukherjee = Vice-President, B.N. Rau = constitutional adviser, Ambedkar = Drafting Committee chairman only.
3. Numbers: 389 → 299 members; 2 years 11 months 18 days; 11 sessions; ₹64 lakh; 284 signatures.

example.q: The Constituent Assembly met for the first time on —
example.solution: **9 December 1946**, in the Central Hall of Parliament, with **Dr Sachchidananda Sinha** as temporary chairman.

patterns.name: Borrowed feature ↔ source country
patterns.howToSpot: A feature (DPSP, joint sitting, fundamental duties, concurrent list, writs) is named and its source country asked, often as a correctly-matched pair.
patterns.logic:
1. Memorise the map: FRs/judicial review/impeachment = USA; DPSP/President's election/12 RS nominees = Ireland; Duties/justice ideal = USSR; liberty-equality-fraternity/Republic = France.
2. Structural ones: strong Centre/residuary with Centre/Canada; concurrent list/joint sitting/Australia; amendment procedure/South Africa; 'procedure established by law'/Japan; emergency FR suspension/Germany.
3. In match-the-pairs, eliminate the UK — it never had a written constitution, so 'written constitution from Britain' is always wrong.

example.q: The concept of a **Concurrent List** and the **joint sitting** of the two Houses of Parliament was borrowed from —
example.solution: **Australia** — Australia's Constitution carries a concurrent list of powers and the device of a joint sitting to resolve deadlocks between the two Houses.

patterns.name: Committee ↔ chairman pairing
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights was chaired by', or a four-row match on committees and chairmen.
patterns.logic:
1. Rule of thumb: Nehru = national subjects (Union Powers, Union Constitution, States); Patel = provinces and rights; Prasad = procedure, steering, flag; Ambedkar = Drafting only.
2. Trap: the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities is **Patel**, not Ambedkar.
3. Trap: the Assembly's President is **Rajendra Prasad**, not Ambedkar — Ambedkar chaired only the Drafting Committee.

example.q: Who among the following chaired the **Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities** of the Constituent Assembly?
example.solution: **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**. He also chaired the Provincial Constitution Committee; the Drafting Committee was Ambedkar's.

patterns.name: Government of India Act 1935 and famous labels
patterns.howToSpot: 'The bulk of the Constitution is drawn from', 'which act provided the federal scheme', plus nickname questions (Mini-Constitution, Magna Carta, heart and soul).
patterns.logic:
1. The single largest source is the **Government of India Act, 1935** — federal scheme, Governors, judiciary, public service commissions, emergency powers.
2. Labels: 42nd Amendment = 'Mini-Constitution'; Part III = 'Magna Carta of India'; Article 32 = 'heart and soul' (Ambedkar); CAG = 'guardian of the public purse'.
3. The Act of 1935 was itself not fully federal in practice — safeguards and reserved subjects stayed with the Viceroy.

example.q: Which one of the following is described as the **'heart and soul'** of the Indian Constitution?
example.solution: **Article 32** (right to constitutional remedies) — Dr Ambedkar's phrase, because the writ power makes the Fundamental Rights real.

subtopics.title: Preamble, Parts and the 12 Schedules
subtopics.concept:
### Preamble
Text-keywords: **Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic**; Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status and opportunity), Fraternity (dignity, unity, integrity). The words **Socialist, Secular and Integrity** were added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**. Justice ideals trace to the Russian Revolution; liberty-equality-fraternity to the French Revolution.

| Case | Holding |
|---|---|
| Berubari Union (1960) | Preamble is not a part of the Constitution |
| Kesavananda Bharati (1973) | Preamble **is** a part; can be amended without altering the basic structure |
| LIC of India (1995) | Reaffirmed Preamble as an integral part |

### Parts of the Constitution (selected)
| Part | Subject | Articles |
|---|---|---|
| I | Union and its territory | 1–4 |
| II | Citizenship | 5–11 |
| III | Fundamental Rights | 12–35 |
| IV | DPSP | 36–51 |
| IV-A | Fundamental Duties | 51A (added by 42nd, 1976) |
| V | The Union (President, Parliament, Judiciary) | 52–151 |
| VI | The States | 152–237 |
| VIII | Union Territories | 239–242 |
| IX | Panchayats | 243–243O (73rd Amendment) |
| IX-A | Municipalities | 243P–243ZG (74th Amendment) |
| IX-B | Co-operative Societies | 97th Amendment, 2011 |
| XI | Centre–State relations | 245–263 |
| XV | Elections | 324–329 |
| XVII | Official Language | 343–351 |
| XVIII | Emergency | 352–360 |
| XX | Amendment of the Constitution | 368 |

Originally **395 Articles, 22 Parts, 8 Schedules**; today about 470 Articles and **12 Schedules**.

### The 12 Schedules
| Sch. | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Names of States and Union Territories |
| 2 | Salaries and emoluments of constitutional office holders |
| 3 | Forms of oaths and affirmations |
| 4 | Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States/UTs |
| 5 | Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes |
| 6 | Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram |
| 7 | Three Lists — Union, State, Concurrent |
| 8 | **22 recognised languages** |
| 9 | Land reform laws (added by 1st Amendment, 1951); judicial review barred till IR Coelho case (2007) |
| 10 | Anti-defection provisions (52nd Amendment, 1985) |
| 11 | **29 subjects** of Panchayats (73rd Amendment) |
| 12 | **18 subjects** of Municipalities (74th Amendment) |

Language additions to the 8th Schedule: **Sindhi** (21st Amendment, 1967); **Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali** (71st, 1992); **Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali** (92nd, 2003) — total 22.

example.q: Which Schedule contains anti-defection provisions?
example.solution: The 10th Schedule (added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985).

tricks.title: Preamble keyword count
tricks.body: Sovereign-Socialist-Secular-Democratic-Republic = 5 descriptors; J-L-E-F = Justice-Liberty-Equality-Fraternity, with only Justice split three ways (social-economic-political).

example.q: Which Preamble ideal is described in three parts?
example.solution: Justice — social, economic and political (Russian Revolution inspiration).

mistakes: Saying the Preamble was amended by the 44th — it was the 42nd (1976).
Listing 18 languages — the count has been 22 since the 92nd Amendment (2003).
Mixing up the 9th Schedule (land reform laws) with the 10th (defection).
subtopics.notes:
### The Preamble — the identity card of the Constitution
The Preamble opens: '**WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA** …', which proclaims that the Constitution draws its authority from the people, not from any king or Parliament. It was framed from **Nehru's Objectives Resolution** (1946). It declares India a **SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC** and promises **justice** (social, economic, political), **liberty** (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), **equality** (of status and opportunity) and **fraternity** (assuring dignity, unity and integrity).

Key facts exams test:
- '**Sovereign**' = no outside power controls India. '**Republic**' = the head of state is elected, not hereditary.
- '**Socialist**', '**secular**' and '**integrity**' were added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976** — the only amendment to the Preamble so far.
- The Preamble is **non-justiciable** — its ideals cannot be enforced in court — and it is **neither a source of legislative power nor a limit on it**.
- Court journey: **Berubari case (1960)** held it is **not** a part of the Constitution; **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** overruled this — it **is** a part, can be amended, but its basic elements cannot be destroyed (basic structure). **LIC of India (1995)** reaffirmed that it is a part.
- The Preamble records the adoption date, **26 November 1949**.

### Parts of the Constitution — the article map
| Part | Subject | Articles |
|---|---|---|
| I | The Union and its territory | 1–4 |
| II | Citizenship | 5–11 |
| III | Fundamental Rights | 12–35 |
| IV | Directive Principles | 36–51 |
| IV-A | Fundamental Duties | 51A |
| V | The Union (President, Parliament, courts) | 52–151 |
| VI | The States | 152–237 |
| VIII | Union Territories | 239–242 |
| IX | Panchayats | 243–243O |
| IX-A | Municipalities | 243P–243ZG |
| X | Scheduled and Tribal Areas | 244–244A |
| XI | Centre–State relations | 245–263 |
| XII | Finance, property, contracts | 264–300A |
| XIII | Trade and commerce | 301–307 |
| XIV | Services | 308–323 |
| XIV-A | Tribunals | 323A–323B |
| XV | Elections | 324–329A |
| XVII | Official language | 343–351 |
| XVIII | Emergency | 352–360 |
| XX | Amendment | 368 |

Part VII (old Part B states) was **repealed** by the 7th Amendment, 1956. **Article 1** names the country: 'India, that is **Bharat**, shall be a **Union of States**'.

### The 12 Schedules
| Schedule | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | States and Union Territories |
| 2 | Salaries and emoluments of constitutional post-holders |
| 3 | Forms of oaths and affirmations |
| 4 | Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats |
| 5 | Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes |
| 6 | Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram |
| 7 | Union (100), State (61) and Concurrent (52) Lists |
| 8 | **22 recognised languages** |
| 9 | Land-reform and other laws protected from challenge (added by 1st Amendment, 1951) |
| 10 | **Anti-defection law** (52nd Amendment, 1985) |
| 11 | Panchayat subjects — 29 items (73rd Amendment) |
| 12 | Municipal subjects — 18 items (74th Amendment) |

In the **I.R. Coelho case (2007)** the Supreme Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule **after 24 April 1973** (the Kesavananda date) can still be reviewed if they destroy the basic structure. The Eighth Schedule's 22 languages include four added by the **92nd Amendment (2003)** — Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.

### Quick revision
- Preamble words order: Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic — all capitalised terms define India's character.
- 42nd Amendment (1976) added socialist, secular, integrity — the only Preamble change.
- Berubari (1960): not a part; Kesavananda (1973): a part, amendable within basic structure.
- Part II citizenship (5–11); Part IV DPSP (36–51); IV-A duties (51A); IX panchayats; IX-A municipalities.
- Schedules 1/12: states-UTs / municipal subjects; 4 = Rajya Sabha seats; 8 = 22 languages; 9 = protected laws (1st Amendment); 10 = defection; 11 = 29 panchayat subjects.
- Article 1: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'.

patterns.name: Preamble keywords and the 42nd Amendment
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment', the order of adjectives, the four ideals and what each promises.
patterns.logic:
1. Added trio = **socialist, secular, integrity** (42nd Amendment, 1976). Nothing else in the Preamble has ever changed.
2. Ideals with brackets: Justice = social, economic, political; Liberty = thought, expression, belief, faith, worship; Equality = status and opportunity; Fraternity = dignity, unity, integrity.
3. Word order: SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC.

example.q: The ideals of **Liberty, Equality and Fraternity** in the Indian Preamble are inspired by the —
example.solution: **French Revolution** (France's constitution supplies these ideals, along with the word 'Republic'); the 'justice' ideal traces to the USSR.

patterns.name: Preamble in the courts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution?', 'can it be amended?', which case decided what.
patterns.logic:
1. Chain of cases: **Berubari (1960) = NOT a part** → **Kesavananda Bharati (1973) = IS a part, amendable but not destructible** → **LIC of India (1995) = reaffirmed part**.
2. The Preamble has been amended **once** (42nd Amendment, 1976) and it survived — proof that it is amendable.
3. It is non-justiciable and neither a source of power nor a prohibition on power.

example.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble **is a part** of the Constitution?
example.solution: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — overruling Berubari (1960), it made the Preamble a part of the Constitution, amendable without damaging the basic structure.

patterns.name: Part ↔ Articles range matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Fundamental Rights are contained in which Articles', 'which Part deals with Municipalities', match-the-column across Parts.
patterns.logic:
1. Learn the five everyday ranges: FRs 12–35, DPSP 36–51, Duties 51A, Panchayats 243–243O, Municipalities 243P–243ZG.
2. Emergency = 352–360; Amendment = 368; Elections = 324–329; Services = 308–323.
3. Odd facts: Part VII stands repealed (7th Amendment, 1956); tribunals = XIV-A (323A-B); citizenship = Part II (5–11).

example.q: Which Part of the Constitution deals with **Municipalities**?
example.solution: **Part IX-A** (Articles 243P to 243ZG), inserted by the 74th Amendment, 1992; Panchayats sit next door in Part IX.

patterns.name: Schedule ↔ content matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'The anti-defection law is in which Schedule', 'which Schedule lists panchayat subjects', correctly-matched schedule pairs.
patterns.logic:
1. Anchors: 8 = 22 languages; 9 = protected laws (1st Amendment 1951); 10 = defection (52nd Amendment 1985); 11 = 29 panchayat subjects; 12 = 18 municipal subjects.
2. Number-memory: 8 → languages, 10 → politicians (defection), 11 → villages, 12 → cities.
3. Ninth Schedule shield is limited: post-Kesavananda laws in it can be reviewed (I.R. Coelho, 2007).

example.q: The **Tenth Schedule** of the Constitution deals with —
example.solution: **Disqualification on the ground of defection** — inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985; it decides when an MLA/MP loses the seat for defying the party.

patterns.name: Eighth Schedule languages
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many languages are in the Eighth Schedule', 'which amendment added Bodo/Dogri/Maithili/Santhali', 'which language was added by the 21st/71st Amendment'.
patterns.logic:
1. Current count: **22 languages** (not 18, not 24).
2. Addition chain: Sindhi — 21st Amendment (1967); Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali — 71st (1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali — 92nd (2003).
3. Classical-language tags are a separate list — do not mix them with the Eighth Schedule count.

example.q: The **92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003** added which four languages to the Eighth Schedule?
example.solution: **Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali**, taking the total count of scheduled languages to 22.

subtopics.title: Fundamental Rights, DPSP and Fundamental Duties
subtopics.concept:
### Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12–35)
Justiciable rights against the State (Art. 12). Six categories after the Right to Property was deleted from Part III by the **44th Amendment (1978)** and made a legal right under **Article 300A**.

| Right | Articles | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| Equality | 14–18 | 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination; 16 equal opportunity in public jobs; 17 abolition of untouchability; 18 abolition of titles |
| Freedom | 19–22 | Art. 19 now has **six** freedoms (property removed); 20 protection on conviction; **21 life and personal liberty** (Maneka Gandhi case, 1978); **21A education for ages 6–14** (86th Amendment, 2002); 22 arrest and detention safeguards |
| Against exploitation | 23–24 | Ban on human trafficking and forced labour; no child below 14 in factories |
| Religion | 25–28 | Freedom of conscience and religion; secular state |
| Cultural and educational | 29–30 | Minority rights to conserve language, script, culture |
| Constitutional remedies | **32** | Writs; called the **"heart and soul" of the Constitution by Ambedkar** |

EWS reservation of **10%** added via **103rd Amendment (2019)** — Articles 15(6) and 16(6).

### Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36–51)
Non-justiciable; borrowed from **Ireland**. Classified: Socialist (38, 39, 41, 42, 43), Gandhian (40 village panchayats, 43, 46, 47 prohibition, 48 cow protection), Liberal-intellectual (44 **Uniform Civil Code**, 45, 50, 51 international peace). Added later: 39A free legal aid, 43A worker participation, 48A environment (all by 42nd Amendment); Art. 45 rewritten by 86th Amendment (early childhood care).

### Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A, Article 51A)
Recommended by the **Swaran Singh Committee (1976)**; **10 duties added by the 42nd Amendment (1976)**; the **11th duty** (parents/guardians to provide education opportunities to children aged 6–14) added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**. Inspired by the **USSR** constitution. Non-justiciable; apply only to citizens.

tricks.title: FR article blocks
tricks.body: 14-18 Equality • 19-22 Freedom • 23-24 Exploitation • 25-28 Religion • 29-30 Culture-Education • 32 Remedies. Count blocks as 5+4+2+4+2+1.

example.q: Under which article is the abolition of untouchability placed?
example.solution: Article 17 — the first article of the Equality block (14-18).

tricks.title: Duty amendment pair
tricks.body: 42nd gave 10 duties; 86th added the 11th (education of 6-14 year-olds). Same 86th also inserted Art. 21A — one amendment, twin gifts.

example.q: Which amendment added the 11th Fundamental Duty?
example.solution: The 86th Amendment, 2002.

mistakes: Treating the Right to Property as a Fundamental Right — it is now Art. 300A, a legal right.
Thinking all FRs suspend in a national emergency — Arts. 20 and 21 never suspend.
Believing DPSPs are enforceable in court — they are non-justiciable.
subtopics.notes:
### Fundamental Rights — the Magna Carta of India
Part III (Articles 12–35) is called the **Magna Carta of India** — borrowed chiefly from the USA. 'State' here (Article 12) means government and its agencies, against which these rights mainly protect you. Six rights exist today:

| Right | Articles |
|---|---|
| Right to Equality | **14–18** |
| Right to Freedom (six freedoms) | **19–22** |
| Right against Exploitation | **23–24** |
| Right to Freedom of Religion | **25–28** |
| Cultural and Educational Rights | **29–30** |
| Right to Constitutional Remedies | **32** |

The old **Right to Property** (Article 31) was deleted by the **44th Amendment (1978)** and demoted to a legal right under **Article 300A**. Article 14 promises equality before law; 15 bans discrimination (with special-care clauses 15(3)–15(6)); 16 guarantees equal opportunity in government jobs; 17 abolishes **untouchability**; 18 abolishes titles. Article 19 carries **six freedoms** — speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession (the property freedom went out with the 44th). Article 21 — **life and personal liberty** — after **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** means any law limiting it must be fair, just and reasonable; **Puttaswamy (2017)** read the **right to privacy** into it. Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes free, compulsory education for ages **6–14** a right. Article 32 gives the **five writs** and is itself a fundamental right — Ambedkar called it the '**heart and soul**' of the Constitution.

### The five writs
| Writ | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Habeas corpus** | 'Produce the body' — against illegal detention |
| **Mandamus** | 'We command' — orders a public authority to do its duty |
| **Prohibition** | Stops a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction (issued during the case) |
| **Certiorari** | Quashes an order passed without/ beyond jurisdiction (issued after) |
| **Quo warranto** | 'By what authority' — challenges illegal occupation of a public office |

High Courts can issue the same writs under **Article 226**, with a **wider** scope (for legal as well as fundamental rights).

### DPSP — Part IV (Articles 36–51), from Ireland
Non-justiciable but '**fundamental in the governance of the country**'. The standard three-way split:

| Group | Key articles |
|---|---|
| **Gandhian** | 40 (village panchayats), 43 (cottage industries), 43B (cooperatives), 46 (SC/ST/weaker sections), 47 (nutrition), 48 (agriculture, cow protection) |
| **Socialist** | 38 (social order), 39 (economic principles), 39A (free legal aid), 41 (work, education, public assistance), 42 (maternity relief), 43A (workers' participation) |
| **Liberal-intellectual** | 44 (**uniform civil code**), 45 (early childhood care), 48A (environment), 49 (monuments), 50 (separate judiciary from executive), 51 (international peace) |

**Minerva Mills (1980)**: the balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP is itself part of the basic structure. Later additions: 39A, 43A, 48A came with the 42nd Amendment; the 86th Amendment (2002) rewrote Article 45 to cover early childhood care below six years.

### Fundamental Duties — Part IV-A, Article 51A
Recommended by the **Swaran Singh Committee**; the **42nd Amendment (1976)** listed **ten** duties, and the **86th Amendment (2002)** added the **eleventh** — parents and guardians providing education opportunities to children aged 6–14. Modeled on the **USSR** constitution. They are non-enforceable by themselves, but courts use them to test reasonableness of laws, and laws can punish their breach (e.g., insult to the flag and anthem under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act).

### Quick revision
- Six FRs, Articles 14–32; property now Article 300A (legal right, 44th Amendment 1978).
- 17 = untouchability; 21 = life and liberty (Maneka 1978; privacy — Puttaswamy 2017); 21A = education 6–14 (86th, 2002).
- Writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto; Art 32 (SC), Art 226 (HC, wider).
- DPSP from Ireland; Gandhian 40/43/46/47/48; socialist 38/39/39A/41/42; liberal 44 (UCC)/45/48A/49/50/51.
- Minerva Mills: FR–DPSP balance = basic structure.
- Duties: Swaran Singh Committee, 42nd Amendment, 10 + 1 (86th) = 11, model USSR.

patterns.name: Article ↔ Fundamental Right mapping
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which Article abolishes untouchability', 'which Article gives the right to constitutional remedies', or a four-row article-right match.
patterns.logic:
1. Learn 14–32 in blocks: 14–18 equality, 19–22 freedom, 23–24 exploitation, 25–28 religion, 29–30 cultural-educational, 32 remedies.
2. Trap: right to property is **not** a Fundamental Right — it sits at Article 300A (44th Amendment, 1978).
3. Single-article favourites: 17 untouchability, 21 life and liberty, 21A education (6–14), 32 writs.

example.q: The abolition of **untouchability** is guaranteed under —
example.solution: **Article 17** — it abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form; Parliament enforces it through the Protection of Civil Rights Act.

patterns.name: Writs: which writ for which situation
patterns.howToSpot: A situation (illegal detention, officer not doing duty, illegal occupant of office) is described and the writ asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Detention → **habeas corpus**; duty not done → **mandamus**; office occupied illegally → **quo warranto**.
2. Court orders: stopping a case midway → **prohibition**; quashing a finished order → **certiorari**.
3. Article 32 = Supreme Court, fundamental rights; Article 226 = High Courts, **wider** (fundamental + other legal rights).

example.q: A person illegally detained by the police should move the court for the writ of —
example.solution: **Habeas corpus** ('produce the body') — the court orders the detaining authority to produce the detainee and justify the detention.

patterns.name: DPSP: classification and article recall
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which of these is a Gandhian principle', 'uniform civil code is under which Article', statements clubbing DPSP with FRs.
patterns.logic:
1. Gandhian = 40 (panchayats), 43 (cottage industry), 43B, 46, 47, 48; Socialist = 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43A; Liberal = 44 (UCC), 45, 48A, 49, 50, 51.
2. 44 = uniform civil code — the evergreen answer.
3. DPSPs are non-justiciable ('not enforceable by any court') but 'fundamental in the governance of the country'.

example.q: **Article 44** of the Constitution, a Directive Principle, provides for —
example.solution: A **uniform civil code** for all citizens — a liberal-intellectual directive; it remains unenforced and is often in the news in debate questions.

patterns.name: Fundamental Duties: count, source, amendments
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many fundamental duties', 'which committee recommended them', 'which amendment added the eleventh duty'.
patterns.logic:
1. Count: **11 duties** today — 10 by the 42nd Amendment (1976), the 11th by the 86th (2002).
2. Source: Swaran Singh Committee recommendation; modeled on the **USSR**.
3. The 11th duty: parents/guardians provide education opportunities to children aged **6–14**.

example.q: The **11th Fundamental Duty**, added by the 86th Amendment, asks every parent/guardian to —
example.solution: Provide opportunities for education to his/her child or ward between the age of **six and fourteen** years.

patterns.name: FR–DPSP conflict and land mark cases
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which case held FRs supreme?', 'balance of FR and DPSP is basic structure', property-right deletion cases.
patterns.logic:
1. **Champakam Dorairajan (1951)**: FRs prevail over DPSPs → led to the 1st Amendment.
2. **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**: basic structure doctrine; **Minerva Mills (1980)**: FR–DPSP balance is basic structure.
3. **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: procedure limiting Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable — not merely enacted.

example.q: Which case held that the **balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles** is part of the basic structure?
example.solution: **Minerva Mills (1980)** — the Court struck down the 42nd Amendment's attempt to give DPSPs primacy over Fundamental Rights.

subtopics.title: Union and State Executive
subtopics.concept:
### The President (Articles 52–62)
| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Election | Indirect: elected MPs + elected MLAs of States, Delhi and Puducherry; single transferable vote, proportional representation; secret ballot |
| Qualification | Citizen, 35 years, qualified to be a Lok Sabha member |
| Oath | Administered by the **Chief Justice of India** (Art. 60) |
| Term / impeachment | 5 years; removal for "violation of the Constitution" (Art. 61) — charge by either House with 2/3 of total membership, other House investigates; 14 days' notice |
| Pardon power (Art. 72) | Pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation; also in **court-martial** cases and death sentences |
| Current (as on 23 Sep 2026) | **Droupadi Murmu, 15th President** (since 25 July 2022; first tribal President) |

### The Vice-President (Articles 63–71)
Elected by **all members (elected + nominated) of both Houses** — the only office whose electoral college includes nominated MPs. Ex-officio **Chairman of Rajya Sabha**. Removal: resolution initiated only in **Rajya Sabha (effective majority)** and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (Art. 67(b)). **C.P. Radhakrishnan is the 15th Vice-President (since 12 September 2025)**.

### Prime Minister and Council of Ministers (Articles 74–75)
- Art. 74: CoM **to aid and advise** the President; Art. 75: appointment, collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha**.
- **91st Amendment (2003)**: CoM capped at **15%** of Lok Sabha / State Assembly strength; defectors barred from ministership.

### The Governor (Articles 153–162)
Appointed by the President for 5 years (holds office at pleasure); pardon power under **Art. 161** (no court-martial power, cannot pardon death sentence); can **reserve bills for the President (Art. 200–201)**; ordinance power **Art. 213**.

tricks.title: Electoral college contrast
tricks.body: President = elected MPs + elected MLAs (no nominated). Vice-President = ALL MPs of both Houses, including the 12 nominated. 'Vice' reaches where 'President' does not.

example.q: Do nominated members of the Rajya Sabha vote in the Vice-Presidential election?
example.solution: Yes — they are excluded only from the President's electoral college.

tricks.title: Pardon ladder
tricks.body: President's Art. 72 pardons court-martial and death sentences; the Governor's Art. 161 covers neither. 'Governor = softer ladder'.

example.q: Can a Governor pardon a death sentence?
example.solution: No — only the President can (Art. 72).

mistakes: Saying the President takes oath from the Vice-President — the CJI administers it.
Assuming the VP's removal starts in the Lok Sabha — it starts in the Rajya Sabha (Art. 67(b)).
Forgetting the 91st Amendment's 15% minister cap and attributing it to anti-defection's 52nd.
subtopics.notes:
### The President — Articles 52 to 62
The President is the **head of the State** (first citizen), while the Prime Minister heads the government. Election (Articles 54–55) is **indirect**, by an electoral college of **elected MPs** and **elected MLAs of the states**, plus elected MLAs of **Delhi and Puducherry** (added by the 70th Amendment). Nominated members and MLCs do **not** vote. The system is **proportional representation by single transferable vote**; vote values are worked out from the **1971 census** (frozen for this purpose). Disputes are decided by the **Supreme Court** (Article 71). Term: **5 years**; oath administered by the **Chief Justice of India**; resignation addressed to the **Vice-President**. Removal is by **impeachment (Article 61)** for 'violation of the Constitution' — no ground is defined, and the charge can be raised in **either House** (special majority of both, investigated under procedure fixed by each House).

The veto family: **absolute** veto (withholding assent), **suspensive** veto (returning a bill once — if passed again, assent is obligatory), **pocket** veto (sitting on a bill — no time limit; used by President Zail Singh on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986). For **state** bills the President has an **absolute** veto (Article 201). Ordinance power — **Article 123**: when Parliament is not in session; must be laid before Parliament; ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles. Pardoning power — **Article 72**: **pardon** (full absolution), **commutation** (substitute a lighter punishment), **remission** (reduce the amount), **respite** (lesser sentence for special reasons, e.g. pregnancy), **reprieve** (temporary stay). It extends to **death sentences, courts-martial and Union-law offences**.

### The Vice-President — Articles 63 to 71
Elected by **all members (elected + nominated) of both Houses** — no state legislatures. Ex-officio **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**; acts as President when the office falls vacant, for a maximum of **6 months**. Removal: a resolution of the **Rajya Sabha by an effective majority (majority of all then members), with 14 days' notice**, agreed to by the Lok Sabha by simple majority.

### Prime Minister and Council of Ministers — Articles 74 to 75
The **real executive**. Article 74 requires the President to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers; the 42nd and 44th Amendments made this advice binding (President may return it once). The CoM is **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3))**; ministers hold office during the President's pleasure. **91st Amendment (2003)**: CoM strength capped at **15% of the Lok Sabha** (minimum **12**); the same cap applies in states. A minister not in Parliament must become one within **6 months**. The **Attorney-General (Article 76)** is the Union's chief law officer — he may speak and take part in **both Houses** but has **no vote**.

### The Governor — Articles 153 to 161
Appointed by the President (not elected); holds office during the President's **pleasure**, though the constitutional term is **5 years**; must be an outsider to the state (convention). Legislative powers include summoning the assembly and **ordinances (Article 213)**; can reserve state bills for the President. Pardoning power (**Article 161**) is **narrower** than the President's: the Governor **cannot pardon a death sentence** (may suspend, remit or commute it) and cannot act in courts-martial cases. The State Council of Ministers follows the same 15% cap (minimum 12) with collective responsibility to the assembly.

### Quick revision
- President: elected MPs + elected MLAs (states + Delhi + Puducherry); PR-STV; 1971 census values; SC decides disputes (Art 71).
- Impeachment Art 61 — 'violation of the Constitution'; either House can start it.
- Vetoes: absolute, suspensive, pocket; pocket used in 1986 (Post Office Bill); state bills = absolute veto of President.
- Art 123 ordinance: 6 weeks from reassembly. Art 72 pardon: death, court-martial, Union law.
- VP: both Houses elect (incl. nominated); RS Chairman; removal only from RS (effective majority, 14 days' notice).
- CoM cap 15% (min 12) — 91st Amendment; AG Art 76 speaks but never votes.
- Governor: pleasure of President; no pardon for death sentence (Art 161).

patterns.name: President's election and impeachment
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who elects the President', 'which members do not vote', 'value of vote based on which census', impeachment grounds/procedure.
patterns.logic:
1. Electors: elected MPs + elected MLAs of states + elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry (70th Amendment). Nominated MPs and MLCs stay out.
2. Method: proportional representation, single transferable vote, secret ballot; values from the **1971 census**.
3. Impeachment (Art 61): charge = 'violation of the Constitution' (undefined); can start in **either House**; needs special majority of both.

example.q: The value of the vote of an MLA in the **Presidential election** is calculated with reference to the population figures of the —
example.solution: **1971 census** — the 42nd and 84th Amendments froze the 1971 base for presidential elections and delimitation alike.

patterns.name: President's powers: veto, ordinance, pardon
patterns.howToSpot: 'The pocket veto was used for which bill', 'which article empowers ordinances', 'the President can pardon which punishments', statement questions mixing the three.
patterns.logic:
1. Vetoes: absolute (withhold), suspensive (return once), pocket (no time limit — Zail Singh, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986).
2. Ordinance = **Article 123**: only when Parliament is not in session; dies **6 weeks after reassembly** unless approved.
3. Pardon (Art 72): death sentence, courts-martial, Union-law offences. Five shades: pardon, commutation, remission, respite, reprieve.

example.q: The so-called '**pocket veto**' of the President refers to —
example.solution: Keeping a bill **without acting on it** — the Constitution sets no time limit for assent; President Zail Singh did this to the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.

patterns.name: Vice-President: election and removal
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who elects the Vice-President', 'how can the VP be removed', 'who acts as President and for how long'.
patterns.logic:
1. Electors = **all members of both Houses** — elected **and** nominated; no state legislatures. This is the key difference from the President's election.
2. Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; acts as President up to **6 months** in a vacancy.
3. Removal only through the **Rajya Sabha**: effective majority + **14 days' notice**, then Lok Sabha concurs by simple majority.

example.q: The Vice-President of India is elected by —
example.solution: An electoral college consisting of **all members of both Houses of Parliament** (elected and nominated) — state legislatures take no part, unlike in the President's election.

patterns.name: PM and Council of Ministers
patterns.howToSpot: Statement questions on collective responsibility, the 15% cap, a non-member minister's 6-month window, the Attorney-General's rights in Parliament.
patterns.logic:
1. Collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha** — Art 75(3); ministers hold office during the President's pleasure.
2. **91st Amendment (2003)**: CoM ≤ 15% of the House, minimum 12 — applies to the Union and to states.
3. A minister who is not an MP must get elected to either House within **6 months**. The AG (Art 76) can speak in Parliament but cannot vote.

example.q: The strength of the Union Council of Ministers is capped by the **91st Amendment** at —
example.solution: **15% of the strength of the Lok Sabha**, with a constitutional floor of **12 ministers** (which includes the Prime Minister).

patterns.name: Governor: appointment, powers, pardon
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Governor is appointed by', 'can the Governor pardon a death sentence', 'who administers the oath to the Governor', reserve-bill questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Appointed by the President; holds office during the President's pleasure; term nominally 5 years.
2. Pardon (Art 161): **no death-sentence pardon** — only suspension, remission or commutation; no courts-martial power.
3. Can reserve state bills for the President (Art 200–201); the President then has an **absolute** veto; ordinances = Art 213.

example.q: Which statement about the Governor's pardoning power is **correct**?
example.solution: Under **Article 161** the Governor can suspend, remit or commute a death sentence but **cannot pardon** it — full pardon of a death sentence belongs to the President alone.

subtopics.title: Parliament and the Judiciary
subtopics.concept:
### Parliament (Articles 79–122)
- **Lok Sabha**: max **530** state seats (the 2 nominated Anglo-Indian seats ended with the 104th Amendment, 2020); term 5 years. Speaker: elected from among members; casting vote; certifies a **Money Bill** (Art. 110); presides over **joint sittings**; pro-tem Speaker appointed by the President to administer oaths. Current Speaker: **Om Birla** (18th Lok Sabha).
- **Rajya Sabha**: max 250 (238 elected + **12 nominated by the President** — literature, science, art, social service); permanent house, one-third retire every 2 years; Deputy Chairman presides in the House.
- **Sessions**: Budget (Feb–May), Monsoon (Jul–Sep), Winter (Nov–Dec). Gap between sessions cannot exceed **6 months**. Quorum: **1/10th** of membership.
- **Joint sitting (Art. 108)**: not for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills; held only **three times** — Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978), POTA (2002).
- Bills: Ordinary, Money, Financial, Constitutional Amendment (Art. 368). **Ordinance power — Art. 123** (ordinance lapses 6 weeks after Parliament reassembles).

### Key committees
| Committee | Strength | Chairman |
|---|---|---|
| Public Accounts Committee | 22 (15 LS + 7 RS) | By convention from the **Opposition**; examines CAG reports |
| Estimates Committee | 30 (all Lok Sabha) | From the ruling party |
| Committee on Public Undertakings | 22 (15 LS + 7 RS) | — |

### Judiciary
- **Supreme Court (Art. 124)**: sanctioned strength **34 judges**; retirement **65** (HC: 62); judges removed by Parliament on "proved misbehaviour or incapacity" via the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 (special majority). Appointments through the **collegium** (Second Judges case 1993). Current CJI: **Justice Surya Kant (53rd CJI, since 24 November 2025)**.
- Jurisdictions: original (Art. 131), writs (32), appellate (132–136), **SLP Art. 136**, review (137), advisory (143), **law of the land binding (Art. 141)**, complete justice (142). Court of record: Art. 129.
- **High Courts: 25**; writ power of HCs (**Art. 226**) is wider than the SC's — it covers fundamental **and other legal rights**. Oldest HCs: Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1862).

### Writs
| Writ | Meaning | Against |
|---|---|---|
| Habeas corpus | "Produce the body" — release from illegal detention | State/individual |
| Mandamus | "We command" — perform public duty | Public official |
| Prohibition | Stops a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction | Judicial/quasi-judicial |
| Certiorari | Transfers/quashes an order of a lower court | Judicial/quasi-judicial |
| Quo warranto | "By what authority" — challenges illegal occupation of a public office | Public office holder |

tricks.title: Committee trio numbers
tricks.body: PAC 22 (opposition chair), CPU 22 (15+7), Estimates 30 (all LS). 'Estimates = 30, exclusively LS.'

example.q: Which parliamentary committee examines the CAG's reports?
example.solution: The Public Accounts Committee (22 members, opposition chairperson by convention).

tricks.title: Writ first letters
tricks.body: **H-M-P-C-Q**: Habeas(body), Mandamus(command), Prohibition(stop-before), Certiorari(quash-after), Quo warranto(by what authority). Prohibition stops a case early; certiorari quashes after.

example.q: Which writ stops a subordinate court from exceeding jurisdiction before it decides?
example.solution: Prohibition (certiorari operates after the order is passed).

mistakes: Believing a joint sitting can resolve a Constitutional Amendment Bill — Art. 108 excludes it.
Saying the Rajya Sabha can be dissolved — it is permanent, with one-third retiring every two years.
Assuming the sanctioned SC strength is 31 — it rose to 34 in 2019.
subtopics.notes:
### Parliament — Articles 79 to 122
Parliament = **President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha**. The Lok Sabha is capped at **552** (530 states + 20 UTs; the two nominated Anglo-Indian seats ended with the **104th Amendment, 2020**). The Rajya Sabha is capped at **250** — 238 elected plus **12 nominated** (literature, science, art, social service). Rajya Sabha members are elected by MLAs by **single transferable vote** (Seat allocation: Fourth Schedule); term is **6 years**, one-third retiring every two years, and it is a **permanent House** — never dissolved. Lok Sabha's normal term is **5 years**. The minimum age is **25** (Lok Sabha) and **30** (Rajya Sabha). A gap between two sessions cannot exceed **6 months**; quorum = **one-tenth** of the total membership. The **Speaker** is elected by the Lok Sabha, resigns to the Deputy Speaker, has a **casting vote**, certifies **Money Bills**, and presides over joint sittings (in the Speaker's absence, the Deputy Speaker Rajya Sabha's Deputy Chairman steps in). **Article 108** provides for **joint sittings** to break deadlocks on ordinary bills — **never** for Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills; only **three** joint sittings have been held (Dowry Prohibition Bill 1960, Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill 1977, POTA 2002).

### Bills and motions
A **Money Bill (Article 110)** contains only the six listed matters (taxes, borrowing, custody of the Consolidated Fund, etc.). It can be introduced **only in the Lok Sabha**, only on the **President's recommendation**, and the Rajya Sabha must return it within **14 days** (it can only recommend). The **Speaker's certificate** is final. Financial Bill-I (Art 117(1)) mixes money and other matters — treat it like an ordinary bill; Financial Bill-II (Art 117(3)) involves expenditure from the CFI but is otherwise ordinary. Motions: **no-confidence** (Lok Sabha only, 50 members' support), censure, adjournment, calling attention, privilege. **Cut motions** — policy cut (₹1), economy cut (specified amount), token cut (₹100). Financial committees: **Public Accounts Committee — 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS), chairman from the opposition by convention**; **Estimates Committee — 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha**; Public Undertakings — 22.

### The Supreme Court — Articles 124 to 147
Sanctioned strength: **34 judges including the CJI**. Judges are appointed by the President; since the **Second and Third Judges cases** the **collegium** (CJI + senior judges) recommends names; the 99th Amendment's NJAC (2014) was struck down in 2015. Qualifications: citizen + (HC judge for 5 years) or (HC advocate for 10 years) or a distinguished jurist; retirement at **65**. Removal: 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity', special majority of both Houses, process governed by the **Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968** (100 Lok Sabha / 50 Rajya Sabha signatures to start). Jurisdiction: **original** (Article 131 — Centre-state disputes), **writ** (32), **appellate** (132–136; Article 136 — special leave to appeal), **review** (137), **advisory** (143 — President may refer questions of law/fact), and **record** (Article 141 — its law binds all courts). **Judicial review** flows from Article 13; the **basic structure** doctrine comes from **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.

### The High Courts and below
Articles 214–231: one HC per state (Parliament may create a common HC). Judges retire at **62**; appointed by the President after consultation with the CJI and the Governor. Courts of subordinate jurisdiction are regulated by the states; **Lok Adalats** (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987) settle disputes by compromise and their awards are deemed decrees.

### Quick revision
- LS max 552, age 25; RS max 250 (12 nominated), age 30, permanent, 6-year terms, STV by MLAs.
- Sessions gap ≤ 6 months; quorum 1/10; Speaker certifies Money Bills; joint sittings: 3, never for Money Bills.
- Money Bill: LS only, President's recommendation, RS 14 days, Speaker's certificate final.
- PAC 22 (15+7, opposition chair); Estimates 30 (all LS, ruling chair by convention).
- SC: 34 judges, retire 65, collegium (99th Amendment struck down 2015); removal = special majority both Houses.
- Jurisdiction map: 131 original, 136 SLP, 137 review, 141 binding, 143 advisory; writs 32/226; HC judge retires 62.

patterns.name: Money Bill and bill procedures
patterns.howToSpot: 'A Money Bill can be introduced only in', 'Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within', 'whose certificate decides if a bill is a Money Bill', statement sets on bill types.
patterns.logic:
1. Money Bill (Art 110): Lok Sabha only, on the President's recommendation; Rajya Sabha gets **14 days** with recommend-only power; the **Speaker's certificate is final**.
2. Joint sitting (Art 108) applies to ordinary (and Financial Bill-I) deadlocks — **never** to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills.
3. The six Money-Bill subjects all concern taxes, borrowing or the Consolidated Fund — check the stem for those words.

example.q: The Rajya Sabha must return a **Money Bill** to the Lok Sabha within —
example.solution: **14 days** — it may only make recommendations, which the Lok Sabha is free to accept or reject; the bill then goes to the President.

patterns.name: Motions and financial committees
patterns.howToSpot: 'A no-confidence motion needs the signature of how many members', 'which committee has members only from the Lok Sabha', cut-motion amounts, PAC chairman convention.
patterns.logic:
1. No-confidence: **Lok Sabha only**, **50 members** to admit; if passed, the ministry resigns.
2. Committees: Estimates = **30, all Lok Sabha**; PAC and Public Undertakings = **22 each (15 + 7)**; PAC chairman from the **opposition** by convention.
3. Cut motions: policy cut ₹1, economy cut a stated sum, token cut ₹100.

example.q: The **Estimates Committee** of Parliament consists of —
example.solution: **30 members, all drawn from the Lok Sabha** (elected by proportional representation); its chairman is appointed by the Speaker from the ruling side.

patterns.name: Parliament's structure: numbers, ages, sessions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha', 'minimum age for the Lok Sabha', 'nominated members of the Rajya Sabha', 'maximum gap between sessions'.
patterns.logic:
1. Numbers: LS 552 (Anglo-Indian nomination ended by the 104th Amendment, 2020); RS 250 = 238 + 12 nominated.
2. Ages: 25 (LS) / 30 (RS); RS term 6 years (one-third retire every 2 years); LS 5 years.
3. Sessions: budget, monsoon, winter; the gap between sessions cannot exceed **6 months**; quorum = 1/10.

example.q: The **Rajya Sabha** can have at most how many members?
example.solution: **250** — 238 representing states and Union Territories plus **12 nominated** by the President for distinction in literature, science, art and social service.

patterns.name: Supreme Court: appointment, removal, jurisdiction
patterns.howToSpot: 'How are SC judges appointed', 'on what ground can a judge be removed', 'which article gives advisory jurisdiction', retirement ages and collegium statements.
patterns.logic:
1. Strength 34 (incl. CJI); appointed by the President on the **collegium's** recommendation (Second/Third Judges cases); NJAC (99th Amendment) struck down in 2015.
2. Removal: 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity', **special majority of both Houses**, procedure under the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968 (100 LS / 50 RS members to move).
3. Jurisdiction anchors: 131 original, 136 SLP, 137 review, 141 law of the land binding, 143 advisory; retire at **65**.

example.q: Under which jurisdiction does the Supreme Court answer **questions of law referred by the President**?
example.solution: **Advisory jurisdiction — Article 143**: the President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance; the Court may report its opinion, which is not binding as a judgment.

patterns.name: High Courts and Lok Adalats
patterns.howToSpot: 'Retirement age of an HC judge', 'who appoints HC judges', 'Lok Adalat award is equivalent to', common High Court questions.
patterns.logic:
1. HC judges appointed by the President after consultation (CJI + Governor); retire at **62** (SC: 65).
2. Article 226 writ power is **wider** than Article 32 — it covers legal rights too.
3. Lok Adalats (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987): awards are **deemed decrees of a civil court**, no appeal on merits.

example.q: Every **Lok Adalat** award is deemed to be —
example.solution: A **decree of a civil court** and is final; it is binding on the parties, and no appeal lies against it on the merits.

subtopics.title: Important Constitutional Amendments
subtopics.concept:
Procedure: **Article 368** — simple majority for some (outside Art. 368), **special majority** for most; ratification by **half the State legislatures** for federal provisions (election of President, extent of executive power, SC/HC, representation of states, 7th Schedule, Art. 368 itself). The **basic structure doctrine** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) limits amendment power.

### Important amendments (PYQ bank)
| Am. | Year | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1951 | Added 9th Schedule; reasonable restrictions on FRs; Arts. 31A, 31B |
| 7th | 1956 | States reorganisation; abolished A/B/C/D class states |
| 24th | 1971 | Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights |

subtopics.notes:
### How the Constitution is amended — Article 368
Amendment power sits in **Part XX, Article 368** (borrowed from South Africa). Three routes:
- **Simple majority** of Parliament (outside Article 368): creating new states, altering state boundaries, citizenship rules, salaries of constitutional functionaries, the Second, Fifth and Sixth Schedules.
- **Special majority** (Article 368 route): majority of total membership of each House **plus** two-thirds of members present and voting — used for most amendments, including Fundamental Rights.
- **Special majority + ratification by half the state legislatures** — for federal provisions: election of the President (54–55), extent of Union/state executive power, Articles 73/162, Supreme Court and High Courts (124–147, 214–231, 241), distribution of legislative power and the Seventh Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself.

There is **no** special convention for joint sittings — a Constitution Amendment Bill never goes to a joint sitting — and the President **must give assent** (24th Amendment). There is no time limit for state ratification.

### The landmarks
| Amendment | What it did |
|---|---|
| **1st, 1951** | Ninth Schedule; Articles 31A/31B; 'reasonable restrictions' on free speech |
| **7th, 1956** | States reorganisation; abolished A/B/C/D state classes; repealed Part VII |
| **24th, 1971** | Parliament can amend **any** part, including Fundamental Rights |
| **42nd, 1976** | '**Mini-Constitution**': socialist, secular, integrity; Fundamental Duties; tribunals; DPSP primacy attempt; LS term extended to 6 years |
| **44th, 1978** | Property deleted from FRs (Article 300A); 'armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance'; emergency approvals tightened; LS term back to 5 years |
| **52nd, 1985** | Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) |
| **61st, 1989** | Voting age **21 → 18** (Article 326) |
| **69th, 1991** | Delhi as **National Capital Territory** |
| **73rd / 74th, 1992** | Panchayats (Part IX, 11th Schedule) and Municipalities (Part IX-A, 12th Schedule) |
| **86th, 2002** | Article 21A (education 6–14); Article 45 rewritten; 11th Fundamental Duty |
| **91st, 2003** | Council of Ministers capped at 15% (min 12); defection bar tightened |
| **92nd, 2003** | Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali added to the Eighth Schedule (22 languages) |
| **97th, 2011** | Cooperative societies — new Part IX-B; 'cooperative societies' added to Article 19(1)(c) |
| **99th, 2014** | NJAC — struck down by the Supreme Court (2015) |
| **100th, 2015** | India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement |
| **101st, 2016** | **GST** (Articles 246A, 269A, 279A — GST Council) |
| **102nd, 2018** | National Commission for Backward Classes given constitutional status (Article 338B) |
| **103rd, 2019** | **10% reservation for EWS** (Articles 15(6), 16(6)) |
| **104th, 2020** | Ended Anglo-Indian nomination; extended SC/ST reservation in legislatures |
| **105th, 2021** | Restored states' power to identify SEBCs (OBCs) |
| **106th, 2023** | **One-third seats for women** in Lok Sabha, state assemblies and Delhi assembly (after delimitation, for 15 years) |

The most recent number to remember: **106 amendments so far** (the 106th was enacted in September 2023).

### Quick revision
- Three routes: simple majority (outside 368), special majority, special majority + half-state ratification.
- Ratification list = federal items: President's election, SC/HCs, Seventh Schedule, state representation, Article 368.
- 42nd = Mini-Constitution; 44th = property out, 'armed rebellion' in; 52nd = defection; 61st = vote at 18.
- 73/74 = PRI + Municipalities; 86 = 21A + 11th duty; 101 = GST; 103 = EWS 10%; 106 = women's one-third.
- Constitutional Amendment Bills: no joint sitting; President's assent obligatory (24th Amendment).

patterns.name: Amendment procedure and state ratification
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which provisions need ratification by half the states', 'what majority amends Fundamental Rights', statement sets on Article 368.
patterns.logic:
1. Special majority = majority of **total membership** of each House + **two-thirds present and voting**; Fundamental Rights are amended by this route.
2. Ratification (half the state legislatures) is needed only for **federal** items: President's election, SC/HCs, Seventh Schedule, state representation in Parliament, Union-state executive power, Article 368.
3. Simple-majority items (new states, boundaries) sit **outside** Article 368; a Constitutional Amendment Bill never goes to a joint sitting.

example.q: Amendment of which of the following requires **ratification by at least half of the state legislatures**?
example.solution: Any change touching **federal provisions** — e.g. the election of the President, the Seventh Schedule, or the representation of states in Parliament (besides a special majority in Parliament).

patterns.name: 42nd and 44th — the twin landmarks
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which amendment is called the Mini-Constitution', 'which amendment removed the right to property', 'armed rebellion replaced internal disturbance by which amendment'.
patterns.logic:
1. **42nd (1976)**: socialist/secular/integrity, Fundamental Duties, tribunals, DPSP-primacy line, LS term to 6 years — the 'Mini-Constitution'.
2. **44th (1978)**: property out of Part III (300A), 'armed rebellion' replaces 'internal disturbance', emergency approval window cut to one month, LS term back to 5 years.
3. The two travel as a pair — 42nd added, 44th corrected.

example.q: The words '**armed rebellion**' in Article 352 replaced which earlier expression?
example.solution: '**Internal disturbance**' — substituted by the **44th Amendment Act, 1978**, to make the emergency ground more specific and serious.

patterns.name: Recent amendments (2016–2023)
patterns.howToSpot: 'The 101st Amendment deals with', 'the 103rd Amendment provides for', 'the 106th Amendment is about', matching amendments 101–106 to provisions.
patterns.logic:
1. **101st = GST**, 102nd = NCBC constitutional status (Art 338B), 103rd = **EWS 10%** (15(6), 16(6)), 104th = Anglo-Indian nomination ended, 105th = states identify OBCs, 106th = **women's one-third reservation**.
2. 99th (NJAC) was struck down — remember it as the amendment that never survived.
3. 100th = India–Bangladesh Land Boundary; 97th = cooperative societies.

example.q: The **106th Constitutional Amendment Act (2023)** provides for —
example.solution: **One-third reservation of seats for women** in the Lok Sabha, state legislative assemblies and the Delhi assembly — to operate after the next delimitation, for 15 years.

patterns.name: Older amendments: one-line recall
patterns.howToSpot: 'Voting age was lowered by which amendment', 'anti-defection law was added by', 'which amendment made Delhi the NCT', 'which amendment added the Ninth Schedule'.
patterns.logic:
1. Numbers ladder: 1st — Ninth Schedule; 7th — states reorganisation; 52nd — defection; 61st — vote at 18; 69th — Delhi NCT.
2. 73rd/74th — PRI/Municipalities; 86th — 21A; 91st — 15% ministry cap; 92nd — four languages.
3. Pair each number with a one-word hook: 61-eighteen, 69-Delhi, 101-GST.

example.q: The voting age in elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies was reduced from 21 to 18 years by the —
example.solution: **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1989**, which amended Article 326.

subtopics.title: Panchayati Raj, Municipalities and Emergency
subtopics.concept:
### Panchayati Raj committees (very common PYQ)
| Committee | Year | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| **Balwant Rai Mehta** | 1957 | **Three-tier** PR system; led to launch at **Nagaur, Rajasthan on 2 Oct 1959** (then Andhra Pradesh) |
| **Ashok Mehta** | 1977 | **Two-tier** system — Zila Parishad + Mandal Panchayat; district as first point of decentralisation |
| **G.V.K. Rao** | 1985 | District the basic unit of planning — District Development Commissioner |
| **L.M. Singhvi** | 1986 | **Constitutional status** for PRIs; Nyaya Panchayats |

### 73rd Amendment (1992) — Panchayats (Part IX, Arts. 243–243O, 11th Schedule)
Three-tier system (two-tier if State population below 20 lakh); **Gram Sabha (243A)**; reservation for SC/ST in proportion and **not less than 1/3rd for women** (many States have raised it to 50% — Bihar first, 2006); 5-year term; **State Election Commission (243K)**; **State Finance Commission every 5 years (243I)**; **29 subjects** in the 11th Schedule.

### 74th Amendment (1992) — Municipalities (Part IX-A, 12th Schedule)
Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation; **18 subjects**; same reservation pattern; District/Metropolitan Planning Committees (243ZD/243ZE).

### Emergency provisions (Part XVIII)
| Type | Article | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| National | **352** | Proclaimed **3 times** — 1962 (China), 1971 (Pakistan), 1975 ("internal disturbance", now "armed rebellion" per 44th Amdt). Approval within **1 month**, renewal every **6 months**; LS can revoke by simple majority; FRs of Art. 19 auto-suspend (Art. 358); only Arts. 20–21 never suspend (Art. 359) |
| President's Rule | **356** | First used in **1959 (Kerala)**; imposed over 130 times; 6-month approval, max **3 years** (conditions after 1 year per **S.R. Bommai case, 1994** — floor test, judicial review) |
| Financial | **360** | **Never imposed** so far |

tricks.title: Committee tier-count rhyme
tricks.body: Balwant-3 (1957), Ashok-2 (1977), Rao-district (1985), Singhvi-Constitution (1986). Decade rhyme: 57-77-85-86.

example.q: Which committee's report led to the Nagaur (Rajasthan) launch of Panchayati Raj on 2 October 1959?
example.solution: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (three-tier recommendation).

tricks.title: Emergency digits
tricks.body: 352-National (3 proclamations: 62, 71, 75), 356-President's Rule (Kerala 1959 first), 360-Financial (zero uses). Approvals: 1 month + every 6 months.

example.q: Which State first faced President's Rule in 1959?
example.solution: Kerala (the elected E.M.S. Namboodiripad government was dismissed).

mistakes: Saying the 73rd Amendment created the Panchayats in 1959 — the 1959 date is only Rajasthan's launch; constitutional status came in 1992.
Mixing 11th Schedule (29 subjects, panchayats) with 12th (18, municipalities).
Claiming a Financial Emergency was declared in 1991 — Art. 360 has never been used.
subtopics.notes:
### Panchayati Raj — Part IX (73rd Amendment, 1992)
Rural local government became a constitutional tier on **24 April 1993** (now **National Panchayati Raj Day**). The framework: **Gram Sabha** (every village, all registered voters) at the base; a **three-tier** system — village panchayat, intermediate (block) panchayat, **Zila Parishad** — though states with under **20 lakh** population may skip the middle tier. Panchayats serve **5-year** terms (dissolved mid-way elections must follow within 6 months). Seats are reserved for **SCs/STs in proportion** to population and **not less than one-third for women** (many states now give 50%). A **State Election Commission** (Article 243K) conducts panchayat elections; a **State Finance Commission (Article 243-I)** reviews panchayat finances **every 5 years**. The **Eleventh Schedule** lists **29 subjects**. Roughly one-third of panchayat seats/chairs are reserved for women by the constitutional minimum.

### The committee ladder
| Committee | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| **Balwant Rai Mehta, 1957** | **Three-tier** democratic decentralisation ('democratic decentralisation' phrase) |
| **Ashok Mehta, 1977** | **Two-tier**: Zila Parishad + Mandal Panchayat |
| **G.V.K. Rao, 1981** | District as the planning unit; 'grass without roots' remark on PRI paralysis |
| **L.M. Singhvi, 1986** | **Constitutional status** for PRIs; Gram Sabha as the base |
| **P.K. Thungon, 1988** | Constitutional recognition; Zila Parishad for planning |

The first panchayat under the 1959 scheme was inaugurated by Nehru at **Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959**. Remember the mapping: Balwant Rai = three-tier, Ashok Mehta = two-tier, Singhvi = constitutional status.

### Municipalities — Part IX-A (74th Amendment, 1992)
In force from **1 June 1993**; Article 243P–243ZG; the **Twelfth Schedule** lists **18 subjects**. Three urban bodies: **Nagar Panchayat** (transitional area), **Municipal Council** (smaller urban area), **Municipal Corporation** (larger urban area). The same 5-year term, reservations, State Election Commission and Finance Commission rules apply; **wards committees** for municipalities with 3 lakh+ population. The **97th Amendment (2011)** added **Part IX-B** on cooperative societies.

### Emergency — Part XVIII (Articles 352–360)
- **National Emergency (352)**: grounds are **war, external aggression, armed rebellion** (the 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance'). Proclamation must be approved by **both Houses within one month** (44th changed it from 2 months); each approval lasts **6 months**, renewable indefinitely by special majority. The Lok Sabha's own term can be extended **one year at a time**. Article **358** automatically suspends Article 19 (only in war/external-aggression cases); Article **359** lets the President suspend enforcement of other rights by order (Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended — 44th Amendment).
- **President's Rule (356)**: failure of constitutional machinery in a state; approval within **2 months**; lasts **6 months** at a time, extendable to **3 years** with conditions (annual parliamentary approval after the first year). **S.R. Bommai (1994)** made proclamations subject to **judicial review** and barred using Article 356 for partisan ends.
- **Financial Emergency (360)**: threatens financial stability; approval in 2 months; salaries of officials including judges can be reduced; **never imposed** so far.

### Quick revision
- 73rd (24 Apr 1993): Part IX, three tiers, Gram Sabha, 29 subjects (11th Schedule), SEC + SFC every 5 years.
- Committees: Balwant Rai = 3-tier (1957), Ashok Mehta = 2-tier (1977), Singhvi = constitutional status (1986).
- 74th: Part IX-A, 18 subjects (12th Schedule), Nagar Panchayat/Council/Corporation, wards committees (3 lakh+).
- National emergency: 'armed rebellion' (44th), 1-month approval, 6-month renewals; Art 19 auto-suspends (358); 20–21 never suspended.
- President's Rule: 2-month approval, 6-month spells, 3-year ceiling; Bommai (1994) = judicial review.
- Financial Emergency (360) has never been proclaimed.

patterns.name: 73rd Amendment structure
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Gram Sabha consists of', 'which article provides a State Finance Commission', 'how many subjects in the Eleventh Schedule', statement sets on PRI structure.
patterns.logic:
1. Base = **Gram Sabha** (all registered voters of the village); tiers = village + intermediate + Zila Parishad (states under 20 lakh may skip the middle tier).
2. Terms 5 years; women's reservation one-third minimum; SEC conducts elections (243K); **SFC every 5 years — Article 243-I**.
3. Eleventh Schedule = **29 subjects**; effective 24 April 1993 = Panchayati Raj Day.

example.q: A **State Finance Commission** is constituted once in —
example.solution: **Five years** under **Article 243-I**, to review the financial position of panchayats and municipalities and recommend tax-sharing and grants.

patterns.name: Committee ↔ recommendation
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which committee recommended a two-tier system', 'constitutional status for panchayats was recommended by', matching four committees to their ideas.
patterns.logic:
1. **Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) = three-tier**; **Ashok Mehta (1977) = two-tier** (Zila Parishad + Mandal Panchayat).
2. **G.V.K. Rao (1981)** = district planning focus; **L.M. Singhvi (1986) = constitutional status + Gram Sabha**; Thungon (1988) = constitutional recognition, district planning.
3. Do not swap the two Mehtas — Balwant = three, Ashok = two.

example.q: Which committee recommended a **two-tier** Panchayati Raj system with Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat?
example.solution: The **Ashok Mehta Committee (1977)** — it wanted the block tier abolished, leaving Zila Parishad at the top and Mandal Panchayat below.

patterns.name: 74th Amendment and urban bodies
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many subjects in the Twelfth Schedule', 'which body for a transitional area', 'wards committees are required for municipalities above what population'.
patterns.logic:
1. Twelfth Schedule = **18 subjects**; Part IX-A; effective 1 June 1993.
2. Body map: transitional area → **Nagar Panchayat**; smaller urban → **Municipal Council**; larger urban → **Municipal Corporation**.
3. Wards committees mandatory for municipalities with **3 lakh+** population (Article 243S); cooperative societies = Part IX-B (97th Amendment).

example.q: For a **transitional area**, the 74th Amendment provides for a —
example.solution: **Nagar Panchayat**; smaller urban areas get Municipal Councils and larger urban areas Municipal Corporations.

patterns.name: National Emergency (Article 352)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Armed rebellion replaced internal disturbance — which amendment', 'within how many days/months must Parliament approve', 'which rights cannot be suspended', 358 vs 359 questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Grounds: war, external aggression, **armed rebellion** (44th Amendment). Proclamation laid before Parliament; approval within **one month**; 6-month renewals, no ceiling.
2. **358**: Article 19 stands suspended automatically in war/external aggression — not in armed-rebellion emergencies.
3. **359**: enforcement of other rights can be suspended by order — but **Articles 20 and 21 never** (44th Amendment).

example.q: Under the 44th Amendment, which Fundamental Rights can **never** be suspended during an emergency?
example.solution: **Articles 20 and 21** — protection in convictions, and life/personal liberty, stay enforceable no matter what the proclamation covers.

patterns.name: President's Rule and Financial Emergency
patterns.howToSpot: 'Approval period for Article 356', 'maximum duration of President's Rule', 'which case made 356 justiciable', 'has a Financial Emergency ever been imposed'.
patterns.logic:
1. Article 356: approval within **2 months**; 6-month spells; ceiling **3 years** (with conditions and annual approvals after the first year).
2. **S.R. Bommai (1994)**: proclamations are open to **judicial review**; majority must be tested on the floor of the House.
3. Article 360 (Financial Emergency) has **never** been used; it can cut salaries, including of judges.

example.q: The famous case holding that a proclamation under **Article 356 is subject to judicial review** is —
example.solution: **S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)** — the Court also laid down that a ministry's majority should be tested on the floor of the assembly, not in Raj Bhavan.

| CAG | **Art. 148** | Constitutional | **K. Sanjay Murthy** (15th CAG, since Nov 2024); term 6 years or 65; audits accounts; reports go to the President/Governor and are examined by the **PAC** |

| NITI Aayog | 1 Jan 2015 (Cabinet resolution) | **Neither constitutional nor statutory** | Chair: PM; Vice-Chair: **A.K. Lahiri** (May 2026); CEO: **Anurag Jain** (Aug 2026); replaced the Planning Commission (1950) |
| NHRC | Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (amended 2019) | Statutory | **Justice V. Ramasubramanian** (since Dec 2024); chair is a former CJI or SC judge |
| Central Information Commission | RTI Act, 2005 | Statutory | **Raj Kumar Goyal** (CIC since 15 Dec 2025); CIC + up to 10 Information Commissioners |
| Central Vigilance Commission | CVCA, 2003 | Statutory | Supervises CBI's work under the Prevention of Corruption Act |
