Key contrasts often asked: **CAG** — ineligible for further Government office after term; **UPSC chairman** — also ineligible; **SPSC chairman** can be made a UPSC member; **AG** is not a full-time government servant; **NITI Aayog** has no statutory backing while the Finance Commission is mandated every **five years**.

example.q: Under which article is the Comptroller and Auditor General appointed?
example.solution: Article 148 (term: 6 years or age 65).

tricks.title: Statutory vs constitutional filter
tricks.body: If the source is a dated Act (1993 NHRC, 2003 CVC, 2005 CIC, 2013 Lokpal) it is statutory; if the source is an Article number it is constitutional; NITI Aayog (Cabinet resolution, 2015) is neither.

example.q: Name one high-profile advisory body that is neither constitutional nor statutory.
example.solution: NITI Aayog.

mistakes: Calling NITI Aayog a statutory body — it is an executive-resolution body.
Saying the 15th FC still governs transfers — from FY 2026-27 the 16th FC (41% share, 2026-31) applies.
Confusing the CAG's examiners — CAG reports are examined by the Public Accounts Committee, not the Estimates Committee.
subtopics.notes:
### Constitutional bodies — the permanent machinery
- **Election Commission (Article 324)**: conducts elections to Parliament, state assemblies, and the offices of President and Vice-President. Since **1993** it is a **multi-member** body — the CEC and **two Election Commissioners** with equal powers. The **CEC can be removed only like a Judge of the Supreme Court**; the other Commissioners, on the **CEC's recommendation**. Tools: the Model Code of Conduct, electoral rolls, recognition of parties, symbols.
- **Union Public Service Commission (Articles 315–323)**: recruits for Union services. Members serve **6 years or till 65**; removal grounds for the chairman mirror a Supreme Court judge's; expenses are **charged on the Consolidated Fund**. State PSCs mirror it (members retire at 62), with a **UPSC-facilitated** removal.
- **Comptroller and Auditor-General (Articles 148–151)**: the '**guardian of the public purse**'. Term **6 years or age 65**; after leaving office, the CAG cannot take any further government post. Audits the accounts of the Union and the states, and bodies substantially financed by them; reports go to the **President/Governor** and are laid before the legislature. The **PAC examines** the CAG's reports (DPC Act, 1971 governs audit duties).
- **Finance Commission (Article 280)**: a **quasi-judicial** body, constituted **every five years** (or earlier); **Chairman + four members** (qualifications set by Parliament's Finance Act, 1951). Recommends the **vertical and horizontal devolution** of central taxes, grants-in-aid (Article 275), and measures to augment state funds for panchayats/municipalities. Its advice is **advisory**, not binding.
- **Attorney-General (Article 76)** and **Advocate-General (Article 165)**: chief law officers of the Union and the state; hold office during pleasure; the AG may speak in Parliament but not vote.
- **Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Article 350B)**; **NCSC (Article 338)** and **NCBC (Article 338B)**; **Official Language rules** sit in Part XVII.

### Statutory and related bodies — know the parent law
| Body | Parent law / note |
|---|---|
| CVC | Statutory from **2003** (earlier executive, 1964; Santhanam Committee advice) |
| CIC | **RTI Act, 2005**; Chief Information Commissioner + Information Commissioners |
| NHRC | **Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993**; chaired by a former Chief Justice of India |
| Lokpal | **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013** |
| NGT | **National Green Tribunal Act, 2010**; fast-track environmental adjudication |
| NITI Aayog | Created by a **Cabinet resolution, 1 January 2015** (non-statutory), replacing the Planning Commission |
| NCW | **National Commission for Women Act, 1990** (set up 1992) |

**Remember the split**: constitutional bodies (EC, UPSC, CAG, Finance Commission, NCSC/NCBC) exist because the Constitution says so; statutory bodies exist because a **law of Parliament** created them; NITI Aayog is neither — it is an executive creation. Exams love asking which is which, and whether a body's expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund (UPSC, CAG — yes).

Exams also ask about **tenure** numbers (6 years or 65 for CEC, CAG, UPSC chairman) and the **removal** ladder (CEC/UPSC-CAG chairman like an SC judge). Names of current office-holders change — revise them separately just before your exam; this lesson sticks to structure.

### Quick revision
- EC: multi-member since 1993 (CEC + 2 ECs); CEC removable like an SC judge; Art 324.
- UPSC: Art 315; 6 years/65; expenses charged; state PSC members retire at 62.
- CAG: Art 148; 'guardian of the public purse'; 6 years/65; no re-employment; reports → President/Governor → PAC scrutiny.
- Finance Commission: Art 280; quasi-judicial; every 5 years; Chairman + 4; advice not binding.
- Statutory vs constitutional: CVC/CIC/NHRC/Lokpal/NGT = statutory; NITI Aayog = executive resolution (2015).
- NCSC Art 338; NCBC Art 338B (102nd Amendment); Special Officer linguistic minorities Art 350B.

patterns.name: Election Commission structure and removal
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many members does the EC have', 'how can the CEC be removed', 'who conducts President/Vice-President elections', statement sets on the EC.
patterns.logic:
1. Multi-member since **1993**: CEC + **two Election Commissioners**, all with equal powers.
2. Removal ladder: CEC — like a **Supreme Court judge**; other ECs — on the **CEC's recommendation**.
3. Jurisdiction: Parliament, state legislatures, and the **President and Vice-President elections**. Local-body elections belong to the State Election Commissions, not the EC.

example.q: The **Chief Election Commissioner** can be removed —
example.solution: In the **same manner as a Judge of the Supreme Court** — by Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, through a special-majority process.

patterns.name: UPSC and CAG: tenure and features
patterns.howToSpot: 'The CAG is called the guardian of', 'UPSC members' tenure', 'who audits the accounts of the states', which expenses are charged on the CFI.
patterns.logic:
1. UPSC: Article 315; members serve **6 years or till 65**; expenses **charged** on the CFI.
2. CAG: Article 148; **6 years or 65**; audits Union and state accounts; barred from further government office; reports to the President/Governor.
3. PAC (22 members, opposition chairman) examines the CAG's reports — 'friend, philosopher and guide of the PAC'.

example.q: The **Comptroller and Auditor-General** of India is appointed by the President under Article —
example.solution: **Article 148**; his removal mirrors that of a Supreme Court judge, and the Constitution bars him from any further office under the Government of India or a state after retirement.

patterns.name: Finance Commission
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Finance Commission is constituted every', 'who decides tax devolution', 'how many members', 'is its advice binding'.
patterns.logic:
1. Article 280: quasi-judicial, **every five years**; **Chairman + four members**.
2. Job: split central taxes between Centre and states (vertical) and among states (horizontal), grants-in-aid, and measures to augment state funds for local bodies.
3. Its recommendations are **advisory** — the government is not bound, though it normally follows them.

example.q: The **Finance Commission** is normally constituted once in —
example.solution: **Every five years** under **Article 280**; it is a quasi-judicial body with a Chairman and four members appointed by the President.

patterns.name: Constitutional vs statutory vs executive bodies
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which of the following is a constitutional body', 'NITI Aayog was created by', 'which act created the CIC/NHRC/Lokpal', odd-one-out sets.
patterns.logic:
1. Constitutional: EC, UPSC/SPSCs, CAG, Finance Commission, NCSC (338), NCBC (338B), Official Language Commission.
2. Statutory: CVC (2003), CIC (RTI 2005), NHRC (1993), Lokpal (2013), NGT (2010), NCW (1990 act).
3. Executive: **NITI Aayog** (Cabinet resolution, 1 Jan 2015) — the trap answer in odd-one-out questions.

example.q: Which one of the following is **not** a statutory body?
example.solution: **NITI Aayog** — it was set up by a Cabinet resolution on 1 January 2015; the CVC, CIC, NHRC and NGT all rest on statutes.

patterns.name: Rights commissions and special officers
patterns.howToSpot: 'NCSC is established under which Article', 'which body looks into linguistic minorities', 'the NCBC got constitutional status by which amendment'.
patterns.logic:
1. NCSC — **Article 338** (SCs and STs); the separate ST commission sits at **Article 338A**.
2. NCBC — **Article 338B**, constitutional status by the **102nd Amendment (2018)**; the 105th (2021) returned SEBC identification to states.
3. Special Officer for **linguistic minorities — Article 350B**; assesses safeguards for language minorities.

example.q: The **National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC)** was given constitutional status by —
example.solution: The **102nd Amendment Act, 2018**, inserting **Article 338B**; the 105th Amendment (2021) restored the states' power to identify OBCs.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Four pairs are offered — an Article with its subject, a Schedule with its content, or an amendment with its provision — and the candidate picks the fully correct set.
pyqPatterns.approach: Hold three tables cold: Parts↔article ranges, Schedules 1–12 content, and the amendment ladder (42 Mini-Constitution, 44 property out, 52 defection, 61 vote at 18, 73/74 local bodies, 86 education, 101 GST, 103 EWS, 106 women). Test each pair; one wrong letter usually knocks out three options.

example.q:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
(a) Tenth Schedule — Municipal subjects
(b) Eleventh Schedule — Panchayat subjects
(c) Ninth Schedule — Languages
(d) Eighth Schedule — Anti-defection
example.solution: (b) — Eleventh Schedule carries the 29 panchayat subjects. Tenth = defection, Ninth = protected laws, Eighth = languages.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who appoints X', 'how is X removed', 'what is X's tenure' — asked for the CEC, CAG, UPSC members, Finance Commission, Attorney-General or the Vice-President.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the removal ladders: CEC/CAG/UPSC chairman — like a Supreme Court judge; other Election Commissioners — on the CEC's recommendation; Vice-President — Rajya Sabha resolution (effective majority, 14 days' notice) concurred in by the Lok Sabha; Governor — holds office at the President's pleasure. Tenure trio: 6 years or 65 (CEC, CAG, UPSC).

example.q: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India holds office for —
example.solution: Six years from assuming office, or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier — and he cannot take any further government office afterwards.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A feature (DPSP, fundamental duties, joint sitting, concurrent list, writs, impeachment) is named and its source country asked, or four pairs are offered.
pyqPatterns.approach: Map it: FRs, judicial review, impeachment — USA; DPSP, President's election, 12 RS nominees — Ireland; duties, justice ideal — USSR; liberty-equality-fraternity, Republic — France; strong Centre, residuary with Centre — Canada; concurrent list, joint sitting — Australia; amendment procedure — South Africa; 'procedure established by law' — Japan; parliamentary system, single citizenship — Britain.

example.q: The idea of **residuary powers with the Union** was borrowed from which constitution?
example.solution: Canada — like Canada, India leaves unlisted subjects to the Centre, and both appoint provincial/state governors from above.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Which is NOT a Fundamental Right / DPSP classification
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options mix real rights with legal/constitutional rights (property under 300A is the classic trap), or ask which directive belongs to the Gandhian/socialist/liberal group.
pyqPatterns.approach: The six rights run 14–32; property is **not** one — it sits at Article 300A (44th Amendment). DPSP groups: Gandhian 40/43/43B/46/47/48, socialist 38/39/39A/41/42/43A, liberal 44/45/48A/49/50/51. Uniform civil code (44) is the evergreen answer.

example.q:
Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right?
(a) Right against exploitation (b) Right to property (c) Right to constitutional remedies (d) Right to freedom of religion
example.solution: (b) — property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978) and survives as a legal right under Article 300A.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A single amendment number (1st, 42nd, 44th, 52nd, 61st, 73rd, 86th, 101st, 103rd, 106th) or a provision is given and the matching half is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Learn the number hooks: 42 = Mini-Constitution, 44 = property out and 'armed rebellion' in, 52 = Tenth Schedule, 61 = vote at 18, 69 = Delhi NCT, 73/74 = PRI and municipalities, 86 = Article 21A, 91 = 15% ministry cap, 101 = GST, 103 = EWS 10%, 106 = women's one-third.

example.q: The voting age in Lok Sabha elections was reduced from 21 to 18 years by which amendment?
example.solution: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1989 — it amended Article 326.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which committee recommended a two-tier panchayati raj' or a Constituent Assembly committee is matched with its chairman.
pyqPatterns.approach: PRI ladder: Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) three-tier, Ashok Mehta (1977) two-tier, G.V.K. Rao (1981) district planning, L.M. Singhvi (1986) constitutional status + Gram Sabha, Thungon (1988) constitutional recognition. Assembly rule: Nehru = union subjects, Patel = provinces and rights, Prasad = procedure/flag, Ambedkar = drafting.

example.q: Which committee first recommended the three-tier Panchayati Raj system?
example.solution: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) — village, block and district tiers; realised in Rajasthan's Nagaur launch of 2 October 1959.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two or three numbered statements about an institution, an emergency provision or a procedure are offered and the candidate picks which are correct.
pyqPatterns.approach: Kill options with one clear error: e.g. 'nominated MPs vote in the President's election' (false), 'joint sitting applies to Money Bills' (false), 'Article 19 auto-suspends in an armed-rebellion emergency' (false — only war/external aggression), 'CAG can accept a post-retirement job' (false). Then check the rest.

example.q: Consider: 1. A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. 2. The Rajya Sabha can amend a Money Bill. Which are correct?
example.solution: Statement 1 only — the Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days with recommendations; it cannot amend.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A situation (illegal detention, an office held without title, a stalled duty) maps to a writ; or an article (123, 161, 213, 72) is matched with ordinance/pardon powers.
pyqPatterns.approach: Writs: habeas corpus = detention, mandamus = duty, prohibition/certiorari = stop/quash a lower court, quo warranto = office title. Pardon spread: Article 72 (President) covers death, courts-martial, Union law; Article 161 (Governor) has no death pardon. Ordinances: 123 Union, 213 state; lapse six weeks after reassembly.

example.q: An ordinance promulgated by the President ceases to operate —
example.solution: Six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless approved earlier; under Article 123 ordinances are valid only while Parliament is not in session.

solvedExamples.q: Which one of the following features of the Indian Constitution has been borrowed from Australia?
options: Federal system with a strong Centre
solvedExamples.solution: The **Concurrent List** (and freedom of inter-state trade, joint sitting) came from **Australia**. Fundamental Rights and judicial review came from the USA, DPSP from Ireland, and a strong-Centre federation from Canada.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Mnemonic for Australia — **CAJ**: Concurrent list, Joint sitting, trade And commerce.

solvedExamples.q:
Consider the following statements about the Constituent Assembly:
1. It held its first meeting on 9 December 1946.
2. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was its permanent President.
3. It adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949.

Which of the statements are correct?
solvedExamples.solution: The Assembly first met on 9 Dec 1946 and adopted the Constitution on 26 Nov 1949 — both correct. Its permanent President was **Dr. Rajendra Prasad**; Ambedkar only chaired the **Drafting Committee**. So statements 1 and 3 are correct.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Ambedkar = Drafting (D), Prasad = President (P) — both start with the right letters.

solvedExamples.q: Which one of the following statements about the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 is correct?
options: It restored the term of the Lok Sabha to five years
It deleted the Right to Property from Part III
It added the words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' to the Preamble
It placed education in the State List
solvedExamples.solution: The 42nd Amendment (called the **Mini-Constitution**) added **Socialist, Secular and Integrity** to the Preamble, inserted Fundamental Duties, moved education/forests/wildlife to the **Concurrent** List and made the Lok Sabha term six years. The term was restored to five years and property was deleted from Part III by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.

solvedExamples.q: Which one of the following bodies is neither a constitutional nor a statutory body?
solvedExamples.solution: **NITI Aayog** (1 January 2015) was created by a **Cabinet resolution** — it has no constitutional article or Act behind it. ECI (Art. 324), Finance Commission (Art. 280) and UPSC (Art. 315) are constitutional bodies; NHRC, CVC, CIC and Lokpal are statutory.
solvedExamples.shortcut: NITI = 'no instrument of law' — think executive-only body.

practice.q: The method of election of the President of India and the Directive Principles of State Policy have been borrowed from which country?
practice.solution: Both the DPSP and the method of electing the President (indirect election through an electoral college) were taken from the **Constitution of Ireland**. Ireland also gave the provision for nominating 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.
practice.shortcut: Ireland = 'President + Principles' — both P-words pair up.

practice.q: The words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' were added to the Preamble by which Amendment?
practice.solution: The **42nd Amendment, 1976** added these three words to the Preamble and is called the 'Mini-Constitution'. The 44th Amendment later undid several 42nd changes (e.g. property, emergency grounds).
practice.shortcut: SS + I = Socialist, Secular, Integrity — all from '42', the SS regiment number rhyme (SS ~ 42 in shape).

practice.q: Which Article was described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the 'heart and soul' of the Indian Constitution?
options: Article 21 — Protection of life and personal liberty
practice.solution: Ambedkar called **Article 32** (writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court) the heart and soul of the Constitution because it makes the Fundamental Rights actually enforceable. Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto flow from it.

practice.q: How many languages are presently recognised in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution?
practice.solution: **22 languages** — Sindhi (21st Amdt, 1967), Konkani-Manipuri-Nepali (71st Amdt, 1992) and Bodo-Dogri-Maithili-Santhali (92nd Amdt, 2003) took the count from 14 to 22.

practice.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and that too on the recommendation of the President.
2. The Speaker's certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is final.
3. A Constitutional Amendment Bill can be passed at a joint sitting of both Houses.

Which of the statements are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct (Arts. 109, 110). Joint sittings (Art. 108) are **not** available for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills, so statement 3 is wrong. Only three joint sittings have ever been held (1961, 1978, 2002).
practice.shortcut: Remember the two 'excluded' bills: Money and Constitution-amendment — Art. 108 skips both.

practice.q: The writ of 'quo warranto' is issued to:
options: release a person from illegal detention
direct a public official to perform his duty
question the legality of a person holding a public office
quash the order of a lower court
practice.solution: **Quo warranto** literally means 'by what authority' — it prevents a person from unlawfully occupying a public office. Release from illegal detention is *habeas corpus*; commanding performance of duty is *mandamus*; quashing a lower court's order is *certiorari*.
practice.shortcut: warranto ~ 'where is your warrant to hold this post?'

practice.q: As of September 2026, who is the Chief Justice of India?
practice.solution: **Justice Surya Kant** is the **53rd CJI**, sworn in on **24 November 2025** (tenure runs to February 2027). B.R. Gavai (52nd) and Sanjiv Khanna (51st) were his immediate predecessors; D.Y. Chandrachud retired in November 2024.

practice.q: The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023 provides for:
options: one-third reservation for women in the Rajya Sabha
one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies
50% reservation for women in Panchayati Raj institutions
practice.solution: The **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Amendment, 2023)** reserves **one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies** for women; it takes effect after a delimitation following the next census. EWS (10%) was the 103rd Amendment; 1/3rd in PRIs came with the 73rd Amendment.

practice.q: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Finance Commission — a statutory body under Article 280
16th Finance Commission — Arvind Panagariya; award period 2026–31
14th Finance Commission — raised States' share to 41%
practice.solution: The **16th Finance Commission** (chair: **Arvind Panagariya**) covers **2026-27 to 2030-31**; its report was tabled on 1 Feb 2026 recommending a **41%** States' share. The 15th FC covered 2021–26; the Finance Commission is a **constitutional** body; the 14th FC had raised the share to **42%**.
practice.shortcut: Odd-one-out elimination: 15th FC = 2021–26; FC is constitutional; 14th FC = 42% — only option (c) survives.

practice.q: Under Article 243-I, a State Finance Commission is constituted once in how many years?
practice.solution: A **State Finance Commission every five years** (Art. 243-I) reviews the financial position of panchayats and municipalities, on the lines of the central Finance Commission (Art. 280).
practice.shortcut: FC (centre) and SFC (state) both run on 5-year cycles.

practice.q: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right under the Constitution of India?
options: Right to move freely throughout the territory of India
practice.solution: The **Right to Property** was deleted from Part III by the **44th Amendment, 1978** and is now only a **legal right under Article 300A**. The others are Fundamental Rights (Arts. 23–24, 19(1)(d) and 32).
practice.shortcut: 'Property' left the FR list in 1978 — the year of the 44th.
practice.pattern: which is NOT a fundamental right

practice.q: The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 capped the strength of the Council of Ministers at what percentage of the strength of the Lok Sabha (or a State Assembly)?
practice.solution: The **91st Amendment (2003)** limits the Council of Ministers to **15%** of the total strength of the Lok Sabha / State Legislative Assembly; it also barred defectors from becoming ministers.
practice.shortcut: 91 ~ 15: think '91st minute of a match, 15 minutes left'.

practice.q: Which committee recommended a two-tier Panchayati Raj system consisting of Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat?
practice.solution: The **Ashok Mehta Committee (1977)** suggested a **two-tier** scheme — Zila Parishad at the district and Mandal Panchayat (cluster of villages) below it. Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) had recommended **three tiers**, G.V.K. Rao (1985) wanted the district as the planning unit, and L.M. Singhvi (1986) sought constitutional status.
practice.shortcut: Tier count mnemonic: Balwant-3, Ashok-2 ('B-A = 3-2'), Rao-district, Singhvi-Constitution.

practice.q: The Vice-President of India can be removed by a resolution:
options: passed by the Lok Sabha with a special majority
initiated in the Lok Sabha and agreed to by the Rajya Sabha
of the Rajya Sabha by an effective majority, agreed to by the Lok Sabha
passed by both Houses with a two-thirds majority of total membership
practice.solution: Under **Art. 67(b)**, removal is by a resolution of the **Rajya Sabha passed by an effective majority** (majority of that House's total strength), **agreed to by the Lok Sabha**, with 14 days' notice. The VP is not impeached; he also doubles as Rajya Sabha Chairman, hence removal starts in that House.
practice.shortcut: VP removal = RS-first (he chairs the RS), unlike the President's impeachment which can start in either House.

practice.q: Which of the following statements about a Financial Emergency under Article 360 is correct?
options: It has never been proclaimed in India so far
It was proclaimed once, during the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis
It can be proclaimed only on the recommendation of the Rajya Sabha
It automatically ceases after one year
practice.solution: A Financial Emergency (**Art. 360**) has **never been imposed** in India. The 1991 crisis was handled through economic reforms, not Art. 360. Unlike other emergencies there is no automatic one-year expiry provision of the kind stated in option (d); approval and periodic renewal follow Art. 352-style parliamentary approval.

practice.q: The Constituent Assembly of India held its **first meeting** on —
practice.solution: The Assembly first met on **9 December 1946**; it adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and brought it into force on 26 January 1950.

practice.q: The **permanent President** of the Constituent Assembly was —
practice.solution: **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946. Sinha was only the temporary chairman; Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
practice.shortcut: Prasad presided; Ambedkar drafted; Sinha only opened.

practice.q: How many members **signed** the Constitution of India on 24 January 1950?
practice.solution: **284 members signed** on 24 January 1950, the last day of the Assembly. The full post-Partition strength was 299; 389 was the pre-Partition sanctioned strength.

practice.q: The **Directive Principles of State Policy** were borrowed from the Constitution of —
practice.solution: **Ireland** supplied the DPSP idea, the method of electing the President, and the nomination of 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.
practice.shortcut: Irish trio: DPSP, President's election, 12 RS nominees.

practice.q: Which one of the following pairs is **correctly matched**?
practice.solution: Joint sitting (Art 108) is an Australian import. Fundamental Duties are from the USSR; Canada gives residuary powers to the **Centre**, not states; liberty-equality-fraternity came from France.
practice.shortcut: Run each pair against the source map.

practice.q: The principle of **suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency** was borrowed from the Constitution of —
practice.solution: The **Weimar Constitution of Germany** supplied the idea of suspending rights during an emergency. Japan gave the phrase 'procedure established by law'; South Africa gave the amendment procedure.

practice.q: The **Union Powers Committee** of the Constituent Assembly was chaired by —
practice.solution: **Nehru** chaired the Union Powers, Union Constitution and States Committees. Patel handled the Provincial Constitution Committee and the Advisory Committee on rights and minorities.
practice.shortcut: Nehru = 'national' committees; Patel = provinces and rights.

practice.q: The **Objectives Resolution**, which became the base of the Preamble, was moved by —
practice.solution: **Nehru** moved the Objectives Resolution on **13 December 1946**; the Assembly adopted it on **22 January 1947**. It sets out sovereignty, justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about the Constituent Assembly:
1. It was directly elected by adult franchise.
2. It adopted the Objectives Resolution in January 1947.
3. It acted as the provisional Parliament after 1950.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 is wrong — members were elected **indirectly** by provincial assemblies under the Cabinet Mission Plan, not by adult franchise. Statements 2 and 3 are correct.
practice.shortcut: Assembly = indirect election; provisional Parliament till 1952.

practice.q: The federal scheme, office of Governor, and emergency provisions of our Constitution are drawn mainly from the —
practice.solution: The **Government of India Act, 1935** is the single largest source — federal scheme, Governors, federal court structure, public service commissions and emergency machinery.
practice.shortcut: Most of the 'machinery' comes from the 1935 Act.

practice.q: How much time did the Constituent Assembly take to frame the Constitution?
practice.solution: From 9 December 1946 to 26 November 1949 the Assembly worked for **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**, across **11 sessions**, at a cost of about **₹64 lakh**.

practice.q: The words '**socialist**, **secular**' and '**integrity**' were added to the Preamble by the —
practice.solution: The **42nd Amendment Act, 1976** (the 'Mini-Constitution') inserted socialist, secular and integrity into the Preamble. It is the only amendment the Preamble has ever received.

practice.q: In the Preamble, the word '**Justice**' is qualified by the ideals —
practice.solution: Justice is **social, economic and political**; Liberty is of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; Equality is of status and opportunity; Fraternity assures dignity, unity and integrity.
practice.shortcut: Justice = SEP; Liberty = 5 freedoms; Equality = status+opportunity.

practice.q: In the **Berubari Union case (1960)**, the Supreme Court held that the Preamble —
options: Is a part of the Constitution and can be amended
Is not a part of the Constitution
Is enforceable in a court of law
practice.solution: In **Berubari (1960)** the Court said the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution. **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** reversed this and made it a part, amendable within the basic structure.

practice.q: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution —
options: Can be enforced in a court of law
Is a source of legislative power
practice.solution: The Preamble is **non-justiciable** — courts cannot enforce its ideals directly — and it is neither a source of power nor a limit on power. It was amended once, by the 42nd Amendment.
practice.shortcut: Non-justiciable + amended once = the two safe lines.

practice.q: The **Fundamental Duties** were added to the Constitution by inserting Part —
practice.solution: Fundamental Duties sit in **Part IV-A, Article 51A**, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice.

practice.q: Which of the following pairs is **correctly matched**?
practice.solution: Emergency provisions (Articles 352–360) lie in **Part XVIII**. Part IX is Panchayats, XIV-A is Tribunals, and Citizenship is Part II.
practice.shortcut: Check each Part against the article map.

practice.q: The **anti-defection law** is contained in which Schedule of the Constitution?
practice.solution: The **Tenth Schedule** (52nd Amendment, 1985) lists the grounds of disqualification for defection. The Eleventh lists panchayat subjects and the Ninth holds protected laws.
practice.shortcut: Ten = defection; Nine = shield; Eleven = villages.

practice.q: The **Ninth Schedule** was added to the Constitution by —
practice.solution: The **1st Amendment (1951)** created the Ninth Schedule to shield land-reform laws from judicial review. I.R. Coelho (2007) held that laws placed there after 24 April 1973 remain open to basic-structure review.

practice.q: How many languages are recognised in the **Eighth Schedule** at present?
practice.solution: The Eighth Schedule recognises **22 languages**. The last four — Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali — came in with the 92nd Amendment (2003).

practice.q: **Sindhi** was added to the Eighth Schedule by which amendment?
practice.solution: The **21st Amendment (1967)** added Sindhi. The 71st (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali; the 92nd (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.

practice.q: Which Article of the Constitution is called its '**heart and soul**' by Dr B.R. Ambedkar?
practice.solution: **Article 32** (right to constitutional remedies) — Ambedkar's phrase, because without the writ power the other rights would be declarations only.

practice.q: Free and compulsory education for children aged **6 to 14 years** is a Fundamental Right under —
practice.solution: **Article 21A**, inserted by the **86th Amendment (2002)**. Article 45 was rewritten as a DPSP for early-childhood care below six; 51A(k) is the matching parental duty.

practice.q: Which one of the following is **NOT** a Fundamental Right today?
practice.solution: The **44th Amendment (1978)** removed property from Part III and made it a legal right under **Article 300A**. The other three are all Fundamental Rights.
practice.shortcut: Property = Article 300A, a legal right — never Part III.

practice.q: The writ of '**mandamus**' is issued to —
options: Command a public official to perform a public duty
Produce a detained person before the court
Quash an order of a lower court
Question the authority of a person holding office
practice.solution: **Mandamus** ('we command') orders a public authority or official to do a duty it is legally bound to perform. Producing a detainee = habeas corpus; quashing = certiorari; office challenge = quo warranto.

practice.q: Which writ can be issued to a person who occupies a **public office without legal authority**?
practice.solution: **Quo warranto** ('by what authority') asks the occupant to show the legal title to the office. Prohibition stops a lower court mid-case; certiorari quashes its order later.

practice.q: The Directive Principle calling for a **uniform civil code** for all citizens is contained in —
practice.solution: **Article 44** — the flagship liberal-intellectual directive. Article 40 = village panchayats, 48 = agriculture and animal husbandry, 51 = international peace and security.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **Gandhian** Directive Principle?
practice.solution: **Art 43** (village and cottage industries) is Gandhian. 39A is socialist, while 50 and 44 are liberal-intellectual directives.

practice.q: How many **Fundamental Duties** does Article 51A contain at present?
practice.solution: **Eleven** — ten were listed by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice, and the **86th Amendment (2002)** added the duty of parents to educate children aged 6–14.

practice.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution on the recommendation of —
practice.solution: The **Swaran Singh Committee** (1976) recommended the duties; the 42nd Amendment inserted them. The Sarkaria Commission dealt with Centre-state relations.
practice.shortcut: Duties = Swaran Singh; PRI tiers = Balwant Rai Mehta.

practice.q: Which one of the following statements is **correct**?
options: In Champakam Dorairajan, the Supreme Court held Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs
Directive Principles are enforceable by courts like Fundamental Rights
The 42nd Amendment made Fundamental Rights superior to DPSPs
Right to property is still a Fundamental Right
practice.solution: **Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** held FRs prevail over DPSPs — it triggered the 1st Amendment. DPSPs are non-justiciable; the 42nd tried DPSP primacy (struck down in Minerva Mills); property left Part III in 1978.

practice.q: In **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)**, the Supreme Court laid down that any law restricting personal liberty must be —
options: Passed by Parliament by a two-thirds majority
Fair, just and reasonable, not merely enacted procedure
practice.solution: Maneka Gandhi read fairness into **Article 21**: 'procedure established by law' must be right, just and fair — a step toward the American 'due process' idea.

practice.q: The President of India is elected by —
options: An electoral college of elected MPs and elected MLAs
practice.solution: The electoral college has **elected MPs**, **elected MLAs of the states**, and (since the 70th Amendment) elected MLAs of **Delhi and Puducherry**. Voting is by proportional representation, single transferable vote.
practice.shortcut: Elected MPs + elected MLAs (states, Delhi, Puducherry).

practice.q:
Consider the statements about the President's election:
1. Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha can vote.
2. Members of State Legislative Councils cannot vote.
3. Election disputes are decided by the Election Commission.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 2 alone is right. Nominated MPs **cannot** vote (statement 1 wrong); disputes go to the **Supreme Court** under Article 71, not the Election Commission (statement 3 wrong).
practice.shortcut: Only elected members vote; SC decides disputes.

practice.q: An impeachment charge against the President for 'violation of the Constitution' may be preferred —
practice.solution: Under **Article 61** the charge can originate in **either House**, which then investigates; removal needs a **special majority of both Houses**. No ground is defined in the Constitution.
practice.shortcut: Either House may start; both must finish.

practice.q: The **ordinance-making power** of the President is contained in —
practice.solution: **Article 123** lets the President promulgate ordinances when **both Houses of Parliament are not in session**; an ordinance lapses **six weeks** after Parliament reassembles unless approved. Article 213 is the Governor's counterpart.

practice.q: The pardoning power of the President under Article 72 extends to —
options: Death sentences, courts-martial sentences and Union-law offences
Death sentences and Union-law offences only
All sentences passed by any court in India
practice.solution: Article 72 covers **death sentences**, sentences of **courts-martial** and offences against **Union laws**. The Governor's power (Article 161) is narrower — no death pardon, no courts-martial.

practice.q: Which punishment-modifying power **substitutes a lighter form** of punishment for a heavier one?
practice.solution: **Commutation** substitutes one punishment for a lighter one of a different character (e.g. death → life imprisonment). Remission **reduces the amount**; respite awards a lesser sentence for special reasons; reprieve is a temporary stay.
practice.shortcut: Commutation = change character; remission = cut amount.

practice.q: The Vice-President of India can be removed by a resolution —
options: Of the Lok Sabha by special majority
Of the Rajya Sabha by effective majority with 14 days' notice, agreed to by the Lok Sabha
Passed by both Houses by two-thirds of the total membership
Of the Cabinet approved by the President
practice.solution: Removal starts (and effectively decides) in the **Rajya Sabha**: majority of all then members, **14 days' notice**; the Lok Sabha then needs only a simple majority. No ground is specified in the Constitution.
practice.shortcut: VP removal = RS first, 14 days' notice.

practice.q: In the absence of the President, who officiates, and for how long at most?
options: The Chief Justice of India, 6 months
practice.solution: The **Vice-President acts as President** for up to **6 months** (Article 65). If a fresh election cannot happen in that period, Article 71 (as interpreted) allows the term to extend until a new President assumes office.

practice.q: The **91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003** capped the size of the Council of Ministers at —
options: 10% of the strength of the Lok Sabha
20% of the strength of the Lok Sabha
15% of the strength of the Lok Sabha
25% of the strength of the Lok Sabha
practice.solution: The cap is **15%** of the House's strength, with a minimum of **12 ministers**, and it applies equally to state Councils of Ministers. It also barred defectors from ministerial office.

practice.q: Which statement about the **Attorney-General of India** is correct?
options: He must be a member of the Lok Sabha
He is appointed by the Chief Justice of India
His advice is binding on the government
He has the right to speak in Parliament but cannot vote
practice.solution: Under **Article 76** the AG is the government's chief legal adviser, appointed by the President; he may **speak and take part** in either House or their committees but has **no right to vote**.

practice.q: The **Governor** of a state is —
options: Elected by the people of the state
practice.solution: The Governor is **appointed by the President** (Article 155) and holds office during the President's pleasure; the constitutional term is five years — a Canadian borrowing.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Governor can pardon a sentence of death.
2. The Governor can commute a death sentence.
3. The Governor's pardoning power covers courts-martial cases.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Only statement 2 is correct — under **Article 161** the Governor may **suspend, remit or commute** a death sentence but cannot **pardon** it, and courts-martial cases lie wholly outside the Governor's power.
practice.shortcut: Governor: commute yes, pardon no, martial never.

practice.q: A **Money Bill** can be introduced only in the —
practice.solution: Article 110 confines Money Bills to the **Lok Sabha**, and only on the **President's recommendation**. The Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days with recommendations only.
practice.shortcut: Money = Lok Sabha only + President's nod.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Speaker's decision on whether a bill is a Money Bill is final.
2. A joint sitting can be summoned for a Money Bill.
3. A joint sitting has been held three times so far.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong — Article 108 excludes **Money Bills** and Constitution Amendment Bills from joint sittings. The three joint sittings: Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978), POTA (2002).
practice.shortcut: No joint sitting for Money Bills — ever.

practice.q: A **no-confidence motion** in the Lok Sabha requires the support of at least —
practice.solution: **50 members** must stand up to admit the motion (Rule 198); it can be moved only in the **Lok Sabha** against the Council of Ministers as a whole.

practice.q: Which parliamentary committee has **members only from the Lok Sabha**?
practice.solution: The **Estimates Committee** has **30 members, all from the Lok Sabha**. PAC and Public Undertakings each have 22 members (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha).

practice.q: The **maximum strength** of the Rajya Sabha provided by the Constitution is —
practice.solution: Article 80 caps the Rajya Sabha at **250** — 238 representatives of states and UTs plus **12 nominated** members. The present House sits at 245.

practice.q: The maximum **gap between two consecutive sessions** of Parliament cannot exceed —
practice.solution: Article 85: sessions must be held so that **no more than six months** pass between one session's end and the next's start — hence at least two sessions a year.
practice.shortcut: Six-month ceiling = at least two sessions yearly.

practice.q: A judge of the **Supreme Court** retires at the age of —
practice.solution: Supreme Court judges retire at **65**; High Court judges at **62**. Removal before that needs proved misbehaviour or incapacity and a special majority of both Houses.

practice.q: The **advisory jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court flows from —
practice.solution: **Article 143** — the President may refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Court. 131 is original jurisdiction; 136 is special leave to appeal; 141 makes SC law binding on all courts.

practice.q: The **National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC)** set up by the 99th Amendment was struck down by the Supreme Court in —
practice.solution: In the **Fourth Judges case (October 2015)** the Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act as violative of judicial independence (basic structure), restoring the **collegium** system.

practice.q: A judge of a **High Court** is appointed by —
practice.solution: **The President** appoints HC judges after consultation with the CJI and the state Governor (collegium recommendations since the Judges cases). Tenure runs to age **62**.

practice.q: An award of a **Lok Adalat** is —
options: Deemed a decree of a civil court and binding
Subject to a regular appeal on merits
Valid only if confirmed by the High Court
practice.solution: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, a Lok Adalat award is **deemed a civil-court decree**, final and binding on the parties; no appeal lies on the merits.

practice.q: The procedure for amendment of the Constitution is laid down in —
practice.solution: Article 368 (Part XX) contains the amendment procedure — special majority, plus ratification by half the states for federal provisions.

practice.q: Which one of the following can be amended by Parliament **alone, by a simple majority**?
practice.solution: Creating new states or altering boundaries (Articles 2–4) needs only a **simple majority** and lies outside Article 368. The other three need the special-majority route; President's election and the Seventh Schedule additionally need state ratification.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about Constitutional Amendment Bills:
1. They can be introduced in either House.
2. They can be referred to a joint sitting on a deadlock.
3. The President's assent is obligatory after passage.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 2 is wrong — Constitution Amendment Bills **never** go to a joint sitting. They may start in either House (statement 1), and after the 24th Amendment the President **must** assent (statement 3).
practice.shortcut: No joint sittings for amendment bills.

practice.q: Which amendment is popularly called the '**Mini-Constitution**'?
practice.solution: The **42nd Amendment (1976)** touched the Preamble, Fundamental Duties, tribunals, DPSPs and emergency provisions — hence 'Mini-Constitution'. The 44th (1978) partially rolled it back.

practice.q: The **Right to Property** was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the —
practice.solution: The **44th Amendment (1978)** deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, and created **Article 300A** — property remains a legal (constitutional) right, not a Fundamental Right.

practice.q: The **101st Constitutional Amendment Act** is associated with —
practice.solution: The **101st Amendment (2016)** created the GST framework — Article 246A (power to tax), 269A (inter-state levy) and 279A (the GST Council).

practice.q: The **103rd Constitutional Amendment Act (2019)** provided —
options: One-third seats for women in legislatures
practice.solution: The **103rd Amendment** inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) to allow **10% reservation for EWS** in education and public employment. Women's reservation is the 106th; NCBC status is the 102nd.

practice.q: The **National Commission for Backward Classes** received constitutional status under —
practice.solution: The **102nd Amendment (2018)** inserted **Article 338B**, giving the NCBC constitutional rank. Article 338 = NCSC; 338A = NCSC for STs.

practice.q: The **anti-defection law** was added to the Constitution by the —
practice.solution: The **52nd Amendment (1985)** inserted the **Tenth Schedule**, listing disqualifications for defection. The 61st lowered the voting age; the 42nd is the Mini-Constitution.

practice.q: The **voting age** in Lok Sabha and assembly elections was reduced from 21 to 18 years by the —
practice.solution: The **61st Amendment (1989)** amended Article 326. The 69th (1991) made Delhi the National Capital Territory; the 73rd created the panchayat tier.

practice.q:
Match the amendment with its provision:
1. 97th — Cooperative societies
2. 100th — India–Bangladesh Land Boundary
3. 104th — Ended Anglo-Indian nominated seats
Which are correctly matched?
practice.solution: All three are right: the **97th (2011)** added Part IX-B on cooperatives; the **100th (2015)** enacted the Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh; the **104th (2020)** ended the Anglo-Indian nomination to the Lok Sabha.

practice.q: The **Gram Sabha** consists of —
options: All registered voters of the village
practice.solution: Under **Article 243(b)** the Gram Sabha is the body of **all persons registered in the electoral rolls** of a village — the foundation of the panchayat system.
practice.shortcut: Gram Sabha = every voter of the village.

practice.q: The **Eleventh Schedule** of the Constitution contains how many subjects for panchayats?
practice.solution: **29 subjects** (11th Schedule, 73rd Amendment). The 12th Schedule gives municipalities **18 subjects**.

practice.q: A state with a population **below 20 lakh** may —
practice.solution: Article 243B lets states with up to **20 lakh** population skip the **intermediate (block) tier**, keeping a village panchayat + Zila Parishad two-level structure.

practice.q: The committee that recommended **constitutional status** for Panchayati Raj institutions was chaired by —
practice.solution: The **L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986)** asked for constitutional status and a Gram Sabha at the base — ideas realised by the 73rd Amendment. Balwant Rai Mehta wanted three tiers; Ashok Mehta, two.

practice.q: The first Panchayati Raj scheme was inaugurated at **Nagaur, Rajasthan** in 1959 by —
practice.solution: **Nehru** inaugurated the first panchayat at **Nagaur on 2 October 1959**, launching the Balwant Rai Mehta three-tier design in Rajasthan.

practice.q: The **Twelfth Schedule** deals with —
practice.solution: The **Twelfth Schedule** lists **18 municipal subjects** (74th Amendment). Panchayat subjects (29) sit in the Eleventh.

practice.q: A **wards committee** is mandatory within a municipal area having a population of —
practice.solution: **Article 243S**: municipalities with **three lakh or more** inhabitants must constitute wards committees (one or more per ward) for local participation.

practice.q: The phrase '**armed rebellion**' as a ground of National Emergency was substituted for 'internal disturbance' by the —
practice.solution: The **44th Amendment (1978)** replaced 'internal disturbance' with the narrower '**armed rebellion**' and made parliamentary approval due within **one month**.

practice.q: During a National Emergency proclaimed on the ground of **armed rebellion alone**, which Article stands suspended?
options: None — Article 19 suspends only for war or external aggression
practice.solution: **Article 358** suspends Article 19 automatically **only** for war or external aggression. An armed-rebellion emergency leaves Article 19 intact; other rights need an Article 359 order (and 20–21 can never go).

practice.q: Parliament must approve a proclamation of National Emergency within —
practice.solution: The **44th Amendment** cut the approval window from two months to **one month**, by special majority of both Houses; each approval then runs six months, renewable indefinitely.

practice.q: President's Rule under **Article 356** can be continued, with parliamentary approvals, for a maximum of —
practice.solution: Six months at a time, extendable up to **three years** — beyond the first year it needs six-monthly approval plus the special conditions laid down by the 44th Amendment.

practice.q: A **Financial Emergency** under Article 360 has been proclaimed in India —
practice.solution: **Never** — Article 360 remains unused. If invoked, it would authorise the reduction of salaries and allowances of all government servants, including Supreme Court and High Court judges.
practice.shortcut: 360 has never been used — the safe answer.

practice.q: The Election Commission of India became a **multi-member** body in —
practice.solution: Since **October 1993** the Commission has had the **CEC plus two Election Commissioners** with equal powers. (A second commissioner had also been appointed briefly in 1989.)

practice.q: Which statement about the Election Commission is **correct**?
options: It conducts elections to panchayats and municipalities
The CEC can be removed like a Supreme Court judge
It is a statutory body created in 1950 by law
Election Commissioners hold office for 5 years
practice.solution: Article 324 makes the EC **constitutional** (not statutory); local-body elections belong to **State Election Commissions**; the tenure of Commissioners is **6 years or age 65**, whichever earlier.
practice.shortcut: CEC = SC-judge removal; local polls = SEC.

practice.q: Elections to the offices of **President and Vice-President** are conducted by —
practice.solution: Under **Article 324** the EC superintends, directs and controls elections to Parliament, state assemblies — and the offices of President and Vice-President.

practice.q: The CAG of India is described as the '**guardian of the public purse**' because he —
options: Audits the accounts of the Union and the states
practice.solution: The CAG audits all receipts and expenditure of the Union and state governments and bodies substantially financed by them; his reports are laid before the legislatures and examined by the **PAC**.
practice.shortcut: CAG audits — it does not budget or sanction.

practice.q: The tenure of a member of the **UPSC** is —
practice.solution: UPSC members hold office for **six years or until 65**; state PSC members get six years or 62. Expenses of both are charged on the Consolidated Fund.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The CAG can take up another government office after retirement.
2. The CAG audits the accounts of both the Union and the states.
3. The CAG's reports are submitted to the President or the Governor.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 is wrong — the Constitution (Article 148) **bars the CAG** from further office under the Government of India or any state. Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

practice.q: The **Finance Commission** is a —
practice.solution: It flows from **Article 280** of the Constitution — hence constitutional — and is constituted every five years with a Chairman and four members.

practice.q: The recommendations of the **Finance Commission** are —
practice.solution: They are **advisory** — the Union government is not bound to accept them, though in practice it does. The commission also suggests grants-in-aid under Article 275.
practice.shortcut: FC advises; it does not command.

practice.q: **NITI Aayog** was established on 1 January 2015 by —
practice.solution: It replaced the Planning Commission through a **Cabinet resolution** — so it is an **executive**, not statutory or constitutional, body.

practice.q: Which one of the following pairs is **correctly matched**?
practice.solution: The **CIC** was created by the RTI Act, 2005. NHRC rests on the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; the NGT on the NGT Act, 2010; the Lokpal on the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.

practice.q: The **National Commission for Scheduled Castes** is established under —
practice.solution: **Article 338** creates the NCSC (338A covers the ST wing; **338B** the NCBC). Article 340 empowers commissions for backward classes generally.

practice.q: The **Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities** is provided for in —
practice.solution: **Article 350B** — the Special Officer investigates matters concerning safeguards for linguistic minorities and reports to the President. Article 350A covers mother-tongue primary education; 351 directs Hindi's development.
